paragraphs.text:
ON THE TRUE INTEGRITY OF VIRGINITY, TO LETOIUS, BISHOP OF MELITENE

1. Most of those who pursue Christ our Bridegroom (all whom heavenly love has wounded and drawn toward the contemplation of the good) see different forms of the good practised by different people in the Church, and so they set out their praises at length. Some compose hymns to virginity. Others write encomiums of those who discipline the body with fasting and sleeping on the ground. Still others admire the greatness of soul of those who sell their possessions for the Lord's sake. They do not think it necessary to teach how each of these things ought to be pursued, but suppose that praise of them alone is enough for progress in the good

[Notes: On "for progress": the reading [?] … in the Venetian edition and in [?]. On "by others": three manuscripts read "among others."]

— or so they reckon. But to you, Letoius, of one soul with the bishops, I have been eager to set out, as in clear daylight, not a hymn to virginity, nor an encomium of those who sell their possessions, nor praise of those who waste their bodies with fasting, but what each of these things is, and how, when rightly accomplished, it contributes to true virtue. It is not that I mean to direct you toward the contemplation of the good by a study of how the virtues differ, since you already understand these things. Rather, by analysing with you what each of them is by nature, I mean to teach those who through you now hold in their breasts a genuine love of the good, and also the rest of my readers. I want them to learn exactly how the beauty of true virginity is adorned, from what source, and with which colours of virtue, as though it were painted in colours on a panel, so that with the goodwill already in them they may pursue more securely each good they strive for. 2. For virginity is truly a great thing: to put it in a word, it makes a human being like the incorruptible God. Yet it does not travel from bodies to souls. It belongs especially to the bodiless soul, and it keeps bodies uncorrupted by means of the soul's own God-loving virginity. The soul receives an image of what is truly beautiful and is lifted toward it by incorruption as if by a wing. It reasons that like is served by like, and that the incorruptible God is fittingly served only by the incorruption within itself. So it brings in the virginity of the body as a handmaid to serve its own beauty. Wishing always to have the body as its companion, so that it can contemplate God undisturbed, it drives the pleasures of the body that trouble it as far away as possible. It makes self-control in the pleasures of the belly the handmaid of bodily virginity, and makes bodily virginity itself the handmaid of its own. So everything else, restraint in food and the rest of the hard discipline, fights against the pleasures that flow through the senses against the body's virginity. But the soul practises the virginity of the body, out of love for what is beautiful, for no other reason than for its own sake. In this way it keeps its own virginity untouched by any wicked thought and so attains likeness to the incorruptible God, as in a spotless mirror, while he shines his graces from himself upon it, for its beauty and

[Notes: On "of the virtues": the reading "of the natures" is not correct; it seems to have been put for "by itself" [?].]

as the discussion has already shown, and as it will show still more clearly as it goes on, virginity belongs especially to the soul's uncorrupted beauty, and it is for the sake of that beauty that the body's beauties too are laboured for. Most people, however, attend only to the name of virginity and give no thought to true virginity. So I think I must make an effort to point out what it involves to those who long to receive the crown of virginity. Otherwise, neglecting through ignorance the chief good, they may spend their whole life serving the handmaid, and because they never serve her mistress, their bodily virginity will not be adorned with the inner beauty, and after much sweat they will suffer loss. So that each of the things that contribute to the beauty of true virginity may be clearly seen, come, let us consider what goal the virgin looks to as she practises her virginity. Then in each of her movements we will see, as in clear daylight, whether she is aiming at the goal set before her, or whether she sets one target and shoots at another and so misses her own goal. In this way we would learn who is truly a virgin. 3. Let us look at it from the beginning, if you like, and consider how the female stands by nature toward the male, so that we may see the goal of virginity clearly revealed. The Creator wished to fill the world from a few first living creatures, as if from certain original seeds. So from the beginning he laid down the form of the bodily animal as a single root for each species of living thing. He cut this form into male and female, from the rational animal down to every irrational species. He made the female a section cut from the male, and placed in the nature of each section an unspeakable drive toward union with the other. Joining to each other the parts severed from each other in love's irresistible unions, he multiplies through the ages every species of living thing, sprouting from the offspring of those before. He says, "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth." His purpose, I say, was to display the world filled with the human race over the whole earth from one man, Adam, in countless varieties of nations. In the same way he wished it to be seen teeming with untold forms from a single pair of each irrational species: four-footed animals, reptiles, birds, swimming creatures, and all living things together. So he subjects the female to the male's mastery and tames the male by the female's pleasure. The female, taken from the male's side as

[Notes: On "alone": one manuscript reads "still only." On "I will strive": some manuscripts read "I have striven." On "of the inner": one of the Royal manuscripts adds "from" [?].]

a part, he ruled should be obedient to the whole from which it was taken, as to its source. By the necessities of nature he contrived that the male should long for what had been taken from him and pursue union with it, so as to take his own member back into himself through intercourse. In this way he wisely displayed male and female as two from one and again one from two. He made their union with one another pleasant to their bodies by the means already described. He also sowed a deep affection for the offspring that union produces, kindled by the torches of love. He makes the male active in nature, as first in creation, and the female passive, as torn from the male's portion. The female, drawn by affection toward the continuance of her kind, is passive, and he did not want her left helpless. So he fashioned the female to be wholly a drug of pleasure for the male, and by forceful attractions he brings the male to her even for the depositing of seed. He does not lead the female to the male; he leads the male to her as a captive by the female's pleasure. The magnet stone has received in its nature an unspeakable power over iron, and it is not itself drawn to the iron but draws the iron to itself from a distance. In the same way the female body has received an inexpressible power over the male, and draws the male's body to intercourse of its own accord, without, so to speak, the soul within it even knowing. So the Creator wished to help the weaker creature: by the pleasure within her she casts a spell on the male, and has him fighting on her behalf, not only for the sake of begetting children but also out of the very drive for intercourse. This is why "A man shall leave his father and his mother." It is not the female who leaves but the male, driven by the drive within him toward intercourse with the female. "And he shall cling to his wife," it says: the husband to the wife, not the wife to the husband, "and the two shall become one flesh." Granting the female sex this power over the one who rules it, the Creator made the very form and appearance of the female body softer. Heard and seen alike, by touch, by glance, by movement, and by the delicacy of all her limbs, she falls upon the male from every side as a soothing balm of pleasure, through every avenue of sense. 4. Since this force is present in our bodies for the reason stated, the virgin

[Notes: On "the power": two Royal manuscripts read "the pleasure."]

sees that souls, through the erotic union of the bodies in which they are bound, take on countless forms of passion. She is always eager to withdraw her soul from attachment to the body, and she commits herself to cutting off the female's relation to the male by turning away from the body toward her own proper good. As she strives to travel this road of virtue, she no longer thinks about the relation her body has to the male. Instead she considers with a keen eye what kinship the soul within her, being bodiless, has with the bodiless God. She kindles the torch of bodiless love far more brightly, and by the sweat she spends for it she strives to show herself stripped of the pleasures of the body and insensible to them. Virginity, then, is something truly divine and belongs especially to the undefiled soul. Such is the relation of male and female bodies to each other. And the virgin carries no stain of female pleasure from the body: she has stripped off all the passions of the flesh and is ambitious to present herself pure to God, whom she has professed to love. Clearly, then, knowing that the kingdom of heaven is the prize of the violent, she must do violence to her own nature for the goal set before her. She must not only master the pleasure that, in a body fashioned like hers, provokes to marriage, but stand firm against every kind of pleasure. For pleasure is one in kind. It gushes up from the flesh like a spring and is divided as if into five channels, the five senses, and through these it flows from within toward the objects of sense [?]. Each of these channels, through its own opening in the sense organs, violently casts its stream upon its own object, washes away whatever is akin to it, and draws it to itself. Then, filled with the mud of the flesh, it flows back again like a torrent from outside through the same openings, more swiftly, into the whirlpools of the flesh. It swamps her soul with passions and carries it under. So the virgin must set reason as a guard over the openings of the senses. She must not simply give them free passage outward, but allow them a measured and quiet one. Otherwise, pouring out unchecked toward whatever they want, they may sometimes swamp the soul floating on them and drag it down to their own concerns. As for the stream that comes back in upon her from outside, she must filter it by squeezing it through the openings, and let it through to the soul clean of all filth. Otherwise, swollen with the mud of the flesh [?], it will churn her up and muddy her entirely with its own defilements.

5. So she will not open her eyes indiscriminately to every visible sight. Otherwise she would take in every form of features and shapes without discernment, and through her eyes she would be troubled by the fantasies those sights produce. Rather, toward some things she will close the eyes of the soul even while the body's eyes stay open, since this present life needs light. But for the contemplation of the true light and of the beauty it reveals, she will eagerly open the soul's eyes, even though they were shut before. Nor will she submit her hearing to every word without examination. Against base words she will stop her ears, as against the onrush of a foul-tasting draught. But to earnest words, which pour out the pure stream of virtue, she will lend her ears eagerly, wanting to learn. Taste is always gaping for what pleases; she will bridle it with reason and drive it temperately to partake only of what is necessary. Touch is the most servile of all the senses, yet by its own smoothness it bewitches all the rest into pleasure. She will keep it entirely spotless of passions, as far as she possibly can. For touch extends throughout the whole body, over all its surface, not only what appears outside but also what lies deep within, and so it lords it over the soul and drives it to passionate touches. It takes possession above all of the most important part, the hands, and through these, as if through traps, it catches all who fall in. Nor does it leave sight empty of its own sorcery. It roughens sight against confused colours and harsh features, and at the same time confuses it [?]. But toward those that are smooth, well formed, and deceptively shaped in colour and form, it relaxes sight from a distance and smooths it, and so it amply displays its power through sight too. Hearing likewise: touch puts it to flight with harsh sounds, but with soft ones, through the smoothly breathing air, it loosens it deep within, and so through hearing too it accomplishes its own work of pleasure. I pass over taste, since it is wholly touch's nursling. Toward flavours of a different kind it contracts and is disgusted, but toward smooth ones it opens its insatiable reservoirs. And what could one say about the generative parts,

[Notes: … and another manuscript reads "through certain weapons fenced about it"; [?] "through certain weapons fenced about it, more hotly, by the shared sensation of traps" [?]. (76) "For what could one say also about the generative [parts]" [?]]

how touch binds the whole power given them for sowing their own kind in its drugs, and through the shared sensation of their smoothness in touch it leads the human being captive by its pleasure? So sight too has been shown to deceive the soul into pleasure through a kind of touch. With the glances of the eyes, as with bodiless hands, it touches from afar whatever it wishes. What it has no power to touch with the body's hands, it embraces passionately with the eyes' gaze, and through the impressions it has taken it sways the whole body with the fantasies that arise. Hearing too touches soft sounds through touch, and through touch it casts its spell on the soul. In short, every sense shares the body in which it rules, and in the same way shares the touch within that body. Through touch, each sense is levered toward its own particular sweetness, and our whole body, lying wholly in touch, is levered in various ways toward pleasure in general. 6. Touch, then, rules in all the senses, but especially in taste and in the generative parts. One touch is linked to another as in a chain, the ruling touch [?]: one is served, the other becomes a servant. All of them pass on the activity of the senses, through touch, to their queen, pleasure, and so make the soul still more bodily through the passions. The virgin's aim is to show her mind pure of all bodily pleasure. For this reason she must cut off from the soul the touch that most makes it bodily. By removing the vehicle of the touches in the other senses, she may also remove, as far as possible, the fuel they supply for their own pleasures. What, then, most makes the soul bodily through touch and makes the pleasures of the other senses sprout in many forms? I say it is the touch in taste, and the touch that tickles the body passionately toward intercourse. Of these, the touch of taste leads and the touch of intercourse follows. Through the touch in taste, swallowing is constantly flattered into gluttony, and the body is fattened. Tickled uncontrollably by the smooth humours seething in its depths, it is driven in a frenzy toward the touch of intercourse. 7. So a woman who means to master the pleasures of intercourse through virginity must first, and much more, be shown to rule over the pleasure of taste, since taste pumps fuel into the other. For the Creator composed the whole human being of rational and irrational parts, like a kind of centaur in the Greek myth used to explain nature,

[Notes: In the manuscripts the reading was: "For what could one say also about … and still say." The Paris edition: "For what could one also about … and still say." A little later: "whatever it might wish," and "the fantasies arising." [?] Gen. 30.]

and to the upper, human-shaped part, from the head to the breast, he fitted from below the part from the navel and loins, like a horse's nature, beastly in its desires for the belly's pleasures and moved irrationally toward intercourse. He did not wish the rational to be carried off by the irrational part. In his perfect wisdom he allowed the rational, which has the irrational part placed beneath it, to drive it as a charioteer for the needs of nature. Because of this authority given to it, whenever the rational does not lead but is led by the irrational, the Word reproaches the charioteer as one wickedly emptied out from above into the pleasure of the irrational, and says, "They became horses mad for mares; each one neighed after his neighbour's wife." And elsewhere, hinting that the irrational part, from the navel and loins, lords it over the soul, it says, "Behold, his strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly." For when the belly is fattened by taste, the parts beneath it are inevitably moved to their natural activities by the overflowing moisture seething in the depths. The belly, lying above these parts, supplies the fuel that kindles them into frenzy, and swallowing pours down the material from above. First, then, the virgin will master taste, temperately reining in from above the springs of the belly's pleasures and the openings to licentiousness that flow from them. Otherwise, having chosen to remain a virgin, she might prostitute herself without restraint to taste, and without noticing she would foolishly sell off her virginity for a different pleasure of enjoyment. For the virgin's taste too must be virgin. Her swallowing must not be corrupted into pleasure by any flattery of what is pleasant. She must keep herself uncorrupted in this too, and wisely drive the body to the service the soul requires. 8. Yet she guards against falling into the pleasure of taste, and she checks and thins the pleasures that spring from the belly by abstaining from food. In doing so she must not in turn upset the body's needs in the opposite direction. "Do not turn aside," it says, "to the right or to the left." Letting taste loose without restraint on every kind of food is truly harmful, for the reasons already given. In the same way, shutting it off to the point where bodily weakness makes one useless is utterly unreasonable. For extremes, truly, as someone said,

[Notes: One of the Royal manuscripts reads "in his perfect wisdom letting go." On "Behold": some codices read "behold" [?]; one [?] "in his loins." On "them": some codices read "it."]

…of the wise, and in this respect equalities [?]. For just as our horse, bucking from too much feed, carries its charioteer off badly wherever it likes, so through excessive want it hinders him on the road of virtue that lies before him. And just as the charioteer must not fatten it with plenty of feed and then suffer from its disorderly bucking, being carried off in every direction, wholly unable to hold out against its seething and unbending strength, so neither must one who has resolved to travel the road to virtue with it bring its strength down, I mean, to uselessness through excessive want. Otherwise, bound to it once it has grown weak, he will endure endless toil on its behalf. He can neither raise it to the race once it has fallen, nor is he allowed to abandon it, because of his natural bond with it. Instead he is always forced to groan along with it because of their partnership and to labor over the care of its health. And because the one that serves him in the exercises proper to the race is not strong, he goes on to lose through lack of practice much of his own skill. Since, then, we must lead the vehicle joined to our nature to the race of virtue neither slackening it too much nor, again, straining it too hard, it is fitting for this reason to consider both the condition of the body, as it actually is, and the qualities of foods. When the body is in its prime and overflowing with natural heat, we should hold it in further and drive out the heat by means of the foods. Otherwise, by adding rich, juicy foods we increase the fat that is there by nature, or by pouring in wine we kindle the seething prime of the body still more, and truly, as the Greek sage says, channel fire upon fire. Rather, for one in his prime and overflowing with natural heat, let us soberly channel in the pure stream from the springs, damping the flame that seethes in his nature by the opposing power of water and tempering it to gentleness by the reason within us. But for one past his prime and withering, let us bring in the help of food and drink as an ally. In every case we should not only measure the quantity of food prudently against a person's strength, but above all judge its quality wisely. For we shall not attend only to the outward appearance of foods, but shall above all look wisely into the power that lies in their depths. There are not a few things, not only among seeds and pulses but among vegetables too, which, contrary to outward impression, contribute nothing at all as food for the ascetic toward a gentle driving of the horse. Instead they prick the depths of the flesh and produce itching titillations, and so secretly cloud and disturb bodies no less than things that are to be shunned outright. 9. Therefore we shall not use salt either simply and indiscriminately, as some of those devoted to asceticism… wherever it likes. καταϐαλεῖν: three manuscripts read καταϐάλλειν. Shortly after, the Venetian edition reads σθεναρὸν τό; another codex, σθεναρὸν τὸ σῶμα. [?] one of the Royal manuscripts, ἐπιϐαλλόντων [?]. In the same place one of the Royal manuscripts reads ἐπιϐαλλόντων δρόμων.

…we have seen do. Out of excessive self-restraint they push away every relish and take only salt with their bread, in place of all seasoning. But these people do not understand that salts, being generative by nature and producing itchings in the body, stimulate bodies toward intercourse more than other things do. If even in these matters the charioteer must use wise discernment with a view to the need at hand, much more must one carefully distinguish how far the qualities of tree fruits are akin to things admittedly harmful. In every case one should prudently admit only the food necessary for life, and spit out the contrived flattery of relishes, which leads to the baits of pleasure. For if bread strengthens the heart of man, one must not irrationally take relish beyond what the food necessarily requires. [?] Since … we shall not even take salt, which is the seasoning of bread, in a quantity equal to the bread. And if no one would take seasoning equal to the thing it is taken with, how could anyone take relishes in excess of the principal food? For these would no longer truly be relishes of the bread; rather the bread would, conversely, be a relish of them. And again taste will secretly outwit the charioteer by another route, through the variety of dishes, and lead him to pleasure. Then he will be found pursuing once more the very thing he is fleeing through asceticism. Therefore, to put it briefly, just as on a four-stringed lyre there is a good harmony, so here too. Since our bodies are composed of four things, earth and water, air and fire, he will always assist what is lacking by means of food, and soften the dominance of what is in excess by subtraction and by a regimen of exercises. He will test not only the qualities of hot and cold within us, but also those of dry and moist. Adding to some in quantity and subtracting from others, intensifying some qualities and relaxing others by his regimen, altering some and preserving others as they are by nature, he will thus prepare for the soul the four-stringed lyre of our body, I mean, freed from all discord and truly well tuned for the melody of the good. But let this much be said by us concerning the manner of taste, for the sake of those training for the race on behalf of virginity, or rather on behalf of all virtue itself. 10. He shows that, just as the body's… Shortly after, the same codex [?] δελεάσματα.

…dragging the soul's wing downward, so the body's weakness, keeping the soul busy with it and afflicting it, does not let it fly up to heavenly things as it wishes. Through incapacity it not only deprives the soul of the presence of good things it might acquire, but also, through the lack of practice that comes from weakness, strips away the beauty of those already acquired. A fat belly does not beget a subtle mind. I mean a belly fat not by build and nature, but one into which a thickness of food flows abundantly through gluttony, clouding and thickening the mind. In the same way, a belly that is too thin leaves the mind breathless through enervation, and in the body's weakness it extinguishes even the subtle mind already being born. He also shows that one must not reject some foods outright and simply stuff oneself with others. In these matters it is fitting not only to measure the quantity with moderation, since by its abundance it can do the same as the foods rejected, but also to judge the quality, which is often as potent as things manifestly harmful. In short, as those who revere the Word, we must practice asceticism with reason and not with unreason. 11. You shall love your neighbor as yourself, and because of this commandment we eagerly stand by him who said, "I was naked and you clothed me, hungry and you fed me, sick and you visited me." Yet whoever takes care to stand by another while mercilessly maltreating himself when he is sick plays the hypocrite with the commandment. For it is clear that one who does not know how to love himself loves wrongly the neighbor he is eager to care for. And how does he rightly fulfill the commandment who has not judged soundly in the case of his slave, the body? Under the pretext of bringing it into subjection he professed to buffet it, but by his indiscriminate impulse he has wickedly used it up. For how will it any longer be the slave of its master, when it has taken the master himself into the service of the violence it suffered from him? And how will it serve the master in doing good to the brothers, when it has taken as slaves for its own care all who are able to do good? It will no longer serve its master in the movements of virtue. Lying in weakness, it will be an occasion of good deeds for all the rest. Everyone will pity its master for his wretchedness over it, and pity the slave for its incurable maltreatment. For the master can no longer take up his own works because he is preoccupied with it, nor, constrained by his bond to it, does he have any thought of being set free. Nor can the slave, even if it obtains mercy, recover the service it owes its master. Instead each becomes for the other the occasion of an incurable punishment, and they bear the unreason of the one who cast [both] into this prison… Royal codex 2879: ἀποσυλοῦσα. [?] ἐπεσκέψασθε. Two old books [?] κειμένην αὐτῷ. And a little after, τούτου ἀδικίαν.

…[both], an unreason to be branded with infamy both by the president of the games and by the spectators. Having enrolled for a heavenly race, through unreason he failed to notice what he was doing. He not only trained wisely in nothing that the stadium requires, but also unjustly threw down the one that ought to serve him in the race, and foolishly overturned himself along with it. Therefore we must necessarily call out once more to those who buffet the body for the sake of acquiring the good: "Do not turn aside to the right or to the left." For just as turning aside to gluttony is grievous, so throwing the body down into uselessness and weakness through excessive hardship is truly most unreasonable. Abstinence from the pleasures of the belly is not good for its own sake, but because it contributes to the acquisition of the good. But if through excessive abstinence we neglect the very thing for which we approve abstinence from foods, the pattern of our regimen will be turned by unreason into its opposite. Because the instrument is wasted and deranged, we will no longer be able to converse with God through readings and prayers, nor to obey the good by doing good to the brothers. One must therefore also take care of the body, not for the body's sake, but in order to acquire, I mean, a servant for philosophy. Unless we have the body's service docile to philosophy, it is impossible to be equal to philosophical readings, or for the mind, straining together with the body, to apply itself fittingly to prayer, or in general to accomplish anything that belongs to philosophy for the benefit of oneself and of those who share one's life. That is why he says, "I buffet my body and bring it into subjection." When through the vigor of the flesh it wants to rise up against its master, I bring it into subjection with the bruises of self-control, compelling it to acknowledge its master. "For I do not strike it," he says, "so as to make it useless for service by measureless blows. Rather, my aim in buffeting it is to bring it into subjection for its master's service." But one who beats the slave with privations to the point that it becomes not only useless for the master's service but also unable to suffice even for itself, what else has he done but make himself the slave of his slave? For when the body can no longer serve, but lies undone by weakness, the master must serve it. He is always laboring to serve its weakness, and no longer gives thought to his own works… of the one who cast [?].

…of asceticism one must cut away, but preserve what is useful, providing for the acquisition of the good. For food does not commend us to God. "For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." That is why abstinence from foods, too, is adopted with reason. For if you examine abstinence from foods in and of itself, he says: "Neither if we do not eat are we the worse, nor if we eat are we the better." Those who do not eat have nothing more in virtue than those who eat, merely by not eating. Nor do those who eat have less than those who do not, merely by eating, if the virtue within them is equal. Therefore we must pursue everything concerning the body with our eyes on the virtue in the soul. These things are not good in themselves, but they become good when they are adorned by their service to the good. So, that service to the good may not be hindered by the body's weakness, he says, "Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments." As has already been said, one must not channel fire upon fire into a body that is seething and swelling with its prime. So too, when the body is chilled by weakness, one must not pour still more cold upon it to its harm. Rather, just as we use up the natural heat by withdrawing its external fuel, so, when this heat has been spent by toils and is then being extinguished by age or disease, we shall restore it, helping it with kindlings from outside. For in a sick body one must also provide for peace among the four parts from which we are composed, which are present everywhere. Otherwise the hot or the cold within us, or in general any one of the four, may at some point prevail and fill the soul with war and discord and with the frenzy that comes from weakness. But let this much be said, in due measure, concerning one of the senses, taste alone, for the sake of bodily virginity. We must now pass on to the other senses, keeping before us the aim of seeing the true virgin. 15. Those who keep the body virgin by abstaining from food and by other hardships must know that the body is only the handmaid of true virginity, and that it is possible to have a virgin body without having a virgin soul. A glance is enough to imprint images of shameful things on the soul, and a word drugged with pleasure, falling on the ear, is enough to corrupt the mind toward licentiousness. So the one who leads the bride is anxious lest it be not the bodies but the minds of those betrothed to Christ that are corrupted. Therefore the virgin must guard her soul above all, even before her body. She must not guard it with one kind of watch while simply leaving it open to another,

but must keep her heart with all vigilance. Then no word flowing from her voice will drug its hearer toward pleasure, and no word from anyone else, falling in from outside through her hearing, will stir her heart into waves of desire. She must do the same with her glance. She must not look softly, lest through it she send images of pleasure to those who see her, to her own harm. Nor must she allow a glance sent from outside to touch her, lest, struck in the heart by it as by a fiery arrow, she be set ablaze, burning for the images of pleasure. "For you will be," it says, "like a deer struck in the liver by an arrow." Rather, she must repel what comes from outside by the resistance of her own soul's gaze, and offer those who see her the token of her own self-control. For even a meddlesome movement of the eyelids is enough to goad and drive the soul into a frenzy of pleasure, and by it these things agitate the soul [?]. Suppose she fixes her eye passionately on some beauty that her eyes have seen, and her soul, softened by pleasure, takes the imprint of the form she saw, as wax does. The one who made the impression has gone away and keeps to himself, but the form of the one she saw has been sealed into her mind. Always pressing toward its own works, it haunts her soul with images. Therefore the virgin must above all, from the very beginning, not fix her eye intently on anyone. Or, if she does look, she must repel from herself with a resisting force the characters that try to force their way in and be imprinted, so that she is not imprinted with any bodily form through long and habitual looking. And if somehow the impressions of bodily things should get in unnoticed, she must wipe them out of herself by continually remembering good things. As in wax, she must smooth away the impressions written in by the bodily form by turning her mind to divine things, and write in the impressions of holy things by laborious contemplation of them. But if she lets the impressions formed in her remain unbroken in her mind, as in a seal, her mind is necessarily occupied with the form stamped on it. It overlooks all other good things, is always excited by the image of the form within, and is passionately absorbed in enjoying it. Such a woman gains nothing by keeping her body uncorrupted through fasts [?] while her soul [is given over] to the [?]…

…judging it a thing of shame [?] that [her body] should be [?], she preserves it by ascetic practice. Yet with bodiless hands she embraces in thought the beloved imprinted on her and carries him about with her always. What she is ashamed to do with the body for fear of being caught, she is not ashamed to do in her thoughts. Such a woman no one could any longer rightly call a virgin even in body. For since the beloved is inseparably mingled with her in thought, the body too must be shaped to the soul's passions. Moved in sympathy with the movements of the mind, it is corrupted along with its corrupted mistress, and as she dreams of erotic things both waking and asleep, it dreams along with her. When such a passion has seized the soul, abstinence from foods and the rest of the body's hardship are from then on superfluous. It is not the horse that carries the rider off into its own buckings; it is the rider himself who wickedly goads the horse with the passion within him. Some people's bodies have been enfeebled by old age, yet the mind, still sick from the licentiousness that held it before, levers the body beyond its strength toward the fantasy of pleasure. In the same way, in those who have become passionate in soul toward love, even when the body has been enfeebled by ascetic practice, the soul stirs it to its own desires. [?] The passion has not passed from the body's vigor to the soul. It moves wickedly from the soul to what belongs to the body. If, then, a glance becomes the kindling of so great a fire, let us listen to him who calls out: "Let your eyes look straight, and your eyelids nod at what is just; be not snatched away by your own eyelids, nor caught by your own eyes." [?]. According to the higher account of nature, the glance falling upon bodies is a kind of touch. When we gaze too long at people with diseased eyes we catch the disease, and when we turn our eyes to other things that are naturally beneficial we are secretly benefited. In the same way, when we turn our eyes to the tokens of pleasure we fill the mind with the disease of pleasure, just as when we turn them to things truly beautiful we receive benefit into the soul through the eyes. If this is so, it is absurd for the virgin [?] toward disease through the eyes, indiscriminately touching with the touch of the eye the very things she would never dare to touch with her hand. For the touch through the eye, one might say, is a procuress and matchmaker. It goes on ahead from far off, before the touch of the hands. And this touch in turn, I mean the touch of the hands, is a warmer handmaid to the embrace. She who has not fled the first touch, that of the eye, would not afterward flee the touch of the hands either. And she who has in turn become erotically entangled in such a touch could hardly… [?] Editions: ἐμπαθῶν. [?] σου νευέτω.

…be found pure of [?]. When we touch fire, we receive its marks in the burns that form on us. It is impossible for anyone who has touched fire with his hand to show a hand free of its burning action. Either blisters rise all at once at the touch, painfully seething and throbbing, and threaten to break at once into sores, or bitter sores are seen already formed on the hand. In the same way, it is impossible for anyone who has touched the fire of love to show a touch free of its marks. Either, as with the hand's touch, blisters rise secretly on the heart: the bitter passions of love, seething and throbbing and gripped by uncontrollable palpitations, which threaten to break at once into the sores of sin. Or they show the whole heart already ulcerated [?]. "For it is a fire," it says, "burning upon all the members; wherever it comes, it destroys from the roots." Since this fire burns upon all the members, those who have resolved to show the body free of burns must beware of touching any of the members. Otherwise, through touch, they may receive the fire's burning action on a member not only in the part they touched, but into the whole body and into the soul itself. If someone touches only a serpent's tail, the head still turns at once toward the touch on the tail, though it stands so far away with the length of the body in between. And if a toe on our foot stumbles, the hairs on our head stand on end at once. In the same way, a passionate touch, even if it is made only on the hand, draws the whole body, from the head to the tips of the nails, into feeling the pleasure that matches the token of the one who touched [?]. A stone thrown into the water of a cistern stirs not only the part of the water near where it fell, but raises circle upon circle and sometimes drives the waves to the very edges. So too an erotic glance, or a word made effeminate by the blandishments of pleasure, falling violently into the virgin's soul as into pure water, raises one erotic thought upon another as in the depths, and sets her whole soul surging, struck by the image of the one who cast it. 15. Therefore the virgin must above all drive the flatteries of the eyes and of the voice, which are a drug of corrupting pleasure, as far as possible from her own senses. She must block her hearing from within with prudent reasoning, and know how to turn away her eyes, as is natural. For once the eyes and the hearing have found passage to the soul, and have then taken on as accomplice the other flattery, that of the hand, they will surely accomplish their own work with [?]. For just as a soldier who has come upon a city with the military [?] goes around looking for a house to lodge in for himself, and … shut out [?]… "Burning": so six manuscripts; the editions read "lying." Toward the… images.

…shut out by the force of the door, or driven off by the master of the house by some other device, he turns elsewhere. Or else he manages to gain an easy first passage inside and to lay down one of his weapons, a spear, a helmet or a shield. Then, even if he goes out for the sake of his comrades and seems to be outside, he is inside in power through the weapon he laid down, and from then on he makes the house his own and his comrades', whom he soon brings in to live with him. So it is with the fearsome soldier of pleasure and sin. He goes round looking for a house for himself, and either he is shut out at the first entrance and turns elsewhere, or he manages to gain an easy first passage inside through the senses. Then he lays down in the soul one of his weapons: the spear of the glance, I mean, which wounds from afar through the eyes; or the helmet of pleasure, the bewitching word that enters through the hearing; or, as a kind of shield, the touch of the hands that stirs the whole body together toward pleasure. Even if he seems to be outside as far as the act of sin goes, not yet having corrupted the body, he is inside in power, corrupting the mind through the weapon he laid down. And from then on he makes the soul that has received any one of these a house set apart for his own pleasure and for his comrades, the passions. So the first passage through the senses must be shut against the soldier of the flesh. The senses must be barred on every side, like doors or windows, with the bars of endurance, so that he may not climb in more craftily through even one of them and bring in death, his comrade, to live with him. For "death," it says, "has come up through your windows." The senses truly are the windows of the soul. Through them the soul may act like a modest woman, opening them a little and quietly letting in the light of perceptible things from outside so that she can attend to the work at hand. Or, agitated by idle curiosity about things outside, she may act like some unbridled harlot, leaning out toward what delights her, wickedly craning her neck, and falling through them into pleasures. For "leaning out from the windows of her house, whatever young man she sees among the foolish children, lacking sense, passing by," she says to him those things for which she has already made herself wholly ready for licentiousness through the undisciplined and wandering state of her senses. But the modest woman, I say, seats the [?] of her thoughts and senses within, as on a hearth, in the midst of the heart. Whatever is useful for virtue and flows pure of every passion she admits. Whatever is useless and foreign to virtue she wisely shuts out, bracing the windows with the hands of prudence. So those who flee the sin that comes from intercourse must not [?] … shut out.

…become entangled in the dangerous slips that come through these things and occur in them. For the touch that comes through the voice and the glances makes its way secretly toward the touch of the hands. And all of these, holding on to one another as in a chain, become matchmakers for the touch of intercourse. So it is not only the single touch of union that the virgin must carefully keep uncorrupted. She must guard the whole class of touch in its many forms, from which every kind springs up through the senses. Then, quenching with the counter-breezes of chastity the sparks sent from afar by the eyes, the voice and the other movements toward pleasure, she will prudently quench along with them the blaze they kindle. Or rather, by never admitting the kindlings of pleasure in the first place, she will never have the blaze of pleasure kindled in her flesh at all. Let the virgin's hearing and gaze, then, be virgin, and her touch too, and every movement she makes.

16. The whole beauty of the true virgin must be ordered so that she neither strives to parade her natural beauty nor, if she lacks it, wishes to beautify herself. It is truly unbecoming to a virgin, and foreign to the incorruption she professes, to take pride in the features the Creator gave her for comeliness and, parading her beauty as I said, to strive to stir up more lovers of the body toward a fall they will share. It is just as unbecoming, if she has not been fortunate in her looks, to busy herself with the contrivance of adornment as a relish of pleasure for those who see her. The first does not show a chaste mind. She gives herself airs over the Creator's work as if it were her own achievement, and while in prayer she begs the judge of the contest not to bring her into the contest, praying, "Lead us not into temptation," she openly thrusts herself into it by the means she uses to attract lovers. Nor does the second show a chaste mind, conjuring up against herself with counterfeit forms the bait for bodily pleasure that she did not receive. Without realizing it, each of them ruins the good given by God and turns it from the purpose set before her. The beautiful one absurdly damages the beauty of her soul through the beauty of her body. The other received the apparent plainness of her body as a provision for guarding her virginity, but wickedly reshapes it with counterfeit forms into a plot against herself. The opposite ought to happen. The first should despise transient beauty and make the body's beauty not a hindrance to the beauty of the soul but, should it so happen, a help to it, transferring the lovers of her body to the soul. The other, who has no smaller share in what is truly beautiful, should take the freedom from temptation that comes with her supposed plainness as a calm for practising the ageless beauty of true virginity [?]…

…and so from now on she rivals the other in immortal beauties, which are her own achievements, while in bodily beauty time will show that she differs from her not at all.

17. Nor is it easy to see what aim these women have in adorning themselves. If it is to assist the purpose of virginity, they are actually doing the opposite of what they profess, absurdly training more assailants against themselves by their adornment. If it is simply to seem beautiful, that looks irrational, unless they mean to give their supposed beauty its fill with the very people from whom they are so eager to win admiration, since they take such care over it. And if it is in order actually to win those they are eager to please, they will plainly show, I say, that they have sunk to the opposite, and will be seen as harlots instead of virgins. Or perhaps they are caught in the middle and pulled apart between two desires. They want to have their fill of lovers outside, and for this reason they strive to make their appearance a relish for common desire, while being held in check by the lover within through shame or fear. For the mind of such women cannot be free of treachery when it incites those outside toward the body by contrivance and wishes to please the one within only by half. Then the mind will no longer be in steady agreement with itself but, as if caught between two battle lines, wretchedly split between the lover within and the one outside. "No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other"; or she will cling to the one, the one outside, adorning herself for him, "and despise" the one within. "The unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord," just as the married woman "cares for the things of the world, how she may please her husband," and "the wife and the virgin are divided." For it is impossible both to care how she may please the one within and to adorn herself for spectators outside, as if on a stage. Picture someone talking with his teacher in the sunlight. He pays no attention to the shadow that follows him, mimicking the movements of his hands and the outlines of his whole figure, but gives himself wholly to his master's conversation. So too the virgin takes no thought for any of the body's images, whether they look comely or ugly, or for the mockery they draw, but turns wholly toward her Master and Bridegroom, and such women converse with him earnestly all their lives in the purest light.

For she "cares how she may please the Lord." And she pleases him by being such as he himself willed to fashion her.

18. So the virgin must not adorn herself, nor make the arrangement of her appearance a relish of pleasure for a licentious gaze. More than that, she must veil her natural bodily beauty as far as she can by her own devices. For, as was said above, the female is a soothing of pleasure for the male. She is fashioned with a gaze more melting than the male's to lure the eye, equipped with a clear voice to charm the ear, and, with the visible softness of her limbs and, in short, the whole shape and movement of her body, formed to beguile with pleasure. A woman, not only when she speaks and looks but even somehow when she sits and walks, draws the male to herself from afar through the natural power over him that is in her, as a magnet, I say, draws iron. For this reason the virgin, guarding against being entangled in any way in the nets of pleasure, must make her eye manly and her voice firm, and in her gait, and in short in every movement of her body, hold back the baits of pleasure. She must not, I say, draw herself further toward pleasure by her devices and make her own body a snare for others and for her own soul alike. Instead she must bravely set herself upright with chaste movements toward the strenuous form of virtue.

19. By removing in herself the pleasure of the female in this way, and cutting off the male's attachment to it, she will make even her outings virgin. She will not behave wantonly by going out continually, nor throw herself into houses beyond what is needful for a virgin. She will make the commandment of the virtue she owes the occasion for every outing. The Lord's commandment will be the charioteer of her going out, and she will choose its times within the seemly part of the day. For she will not simply make the Lord's commandment material for gadding about and for reproach because of him who said, "I was sick and you did not visit me," and the rest. Venturing out at every hour and against all propriety, appearing to the crowds at unsuitable times in every alley, will she not, by failing to use the good of God's commandment skilfully, wickedly turn it into a slander against herself, and her untried youth simply [?]…

For the virgin who has turned away from the bonds of marriage must not simply run with the herd, rushing about everywhere as she pleases, as though she had fled marriage not in order to wait always on the better Bridegroom but in order to be free to go wherever she likes. Nor did she flee partnership with a husband so as to have no witness or judge of her life. Nor did she do it so that, free of jealousy, she might wallow at liberty with whomever she likes, with no one to examine her movements. She did it so that, fleeing the pleasures of the flesh, the pangs of childbirth and the painful, toilsome care of worldly anxieties, she might order her life toward incorruption under God, the witness of her virtue and its jealous guardian. "For I am," he says, "a jealous God": jealous against anyone who commits adultery with my beauty in you and corrupts it. If, having thrown off the yoke of a husband, she becomes useless to the life for which she was fashioned, housekeeping and childbearing, and blameworthy in the virginity she professes as well, it is a total loss. If she is corrupting her soul with undisciplined thoughts and her body with unrestrained friskings, it is far better for her to be joined to a husband and be guided by him through life. Then she will be useful as a help in the house, repaying him for his protection, and will present him with good children to care for him in old age and carry on the family. And in one respect at least, through her husband's jealousy, she will keep virginity for God as far as she can. For the word of truth does not even recognize as virgins those who loiter in alleys and houses without discipline. "For they learn to be idle, going about from house to house; and not only idle but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not."

20. A widow has already had experience of a husband and has grown used to meeting the eyes of men. Yet she must not shamelessly move her tongue and her feet toward anyone she meets, so as not to fall under the charges already mentioned. How much more must the virgin, who has never stripped off the tunic of modesty before a man, keep her tongue reverent and virgin, and take each step strictly as necessity requires? The virgin should say only what will benefit the minds of those who hear it and what, through the apt reply she receives, will further adorn her soul with understanding of divine things. For the stream of speech carried outward by the tongue becomes a witness to the spring it flows from. "For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries," and so on; by its fruits the tree is known. And the true virgin, as from a pure spring, the purity of her character, must pour forth, unclouded by any defilement, [?] [Four manuscripts: "is made known."]

…her speech quietly. It must not only carry no harmful or deceitful meaning tending toward pleasure, but must never show itself idle, coming as it does from a rational soul. For the mind must take its fill of every word drawn uncorrupted from a virgin spring, as of a draught of incorruption, and in return, with modesty, pass on the benefactress [?] to those like her. Such will the virgin be when she speaks, if ever she must speak. For care must be taken over to whom, how and when it is seen to be fitting for her to speak. The virgin's speech must not simply be squandered on whoever happens along, nor again be boldly laid bare before those who deserve reverence. It must not pour out when it meets no need, beyond what befits a virgin. And when need does call it from a virgin's mouth, it must not overflow too lavishly on the occasion the need provides. Rather, she must always take account of the person, the need and the occasion, and when need compels her to speak, she must speak far less than she hears. For nature, too, measuring the usefulness of speech in proportion to hearing, made us two ears but only one tongue, since we ought to listen twice as much for instruction and bring forth speech cut down by half in answer to questions. So, in keeping with nature, with those to whom the virgin speaks at a fitting time she will listen far more than she speaks. Every word of hers will come forth from her lips bringing nothing but benefit to those who hear, or will proceed from her mouth decorously by way of a question, trading for instruction. Everything else will rest quiet in the inner chambers, while she prays continually, far more than others: "Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of enclosure about my lips." In this way she will secure her mouth with prayers. No less will she secure her hearing, so that nothing evil may flow into it from outside. And she will keep the gate of her mind in stillness of hearing and of tongue, always beseeching the Lord: "Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins."

21. Far more blameworthy than anything mentioned so far, and foreign to the virginal character, is for a virgin not only to loiter about houses but also to become a matchmaker for marriages. For "marriage is honorable in all," but it is fitting for others and not for the virgin. Having withdrawn to her own path, she must not be found mixing with the rest of the crowd on the highways of life. For the way of those who hold to marriage is one… [(82) "In keeping with nature": one manuscript reads "if she speaks" [?]. (80) "Whoever happens along": some manuscripts read συντυχόντας, "those she meets."]

…and the path, I say, of those who honor virginity is another. "And the virgin and the married woman are divided." So the virgin must withdraw from matrimonial affairs; or rather, she must not approach them at all in the first place. Let the other women, who have chosen to cherish bridegrooms of flesh, act as matchmakers for those marriages as they see fit, and show their zeal for them, if it pleases them. But let the virgin, always cherishing her own Bridegroom, rather betroth undefiled brides to him for incorruption, if she wishes to make matches at all. Let those women toil over the mortal bridal chamber; but let her dance around the Lord with the wise virgins, her lamp lit, either following the Bridegroom or, by her own light of virginity, betrothing others to virginity too. For it is truly a thing full of shame and reproach for a virgin when women already caught up in marriage urge others toward virginity, while the virgin hurries to make matches. Those women, entangled in the pains of marriage as if through inexperience of what they were getting into, kindly turn the unwed away from going through the same sufferings. They truly call blessed the purity of the Bridegroom and of those wedded to him, in the present life and the life to come, and they urge the unwed toward virginity. But the virgin, I say, hurries to make matches for marriages, and by what she does she shows, I think, the opposite. She shows that, having been bound in advance by her promise of virginity, she is now compelled out of shame to keep up the appearance of it. Inwardly she approves of marriage, and perhaps she regrets the pleasure she has been deprived of. By what she does she shows clearly the disposition toward marriage that she has in her soul, as if she wanted to show the brides openly that she shares their delight in the pleasures they are about to enjoy. Since the virgin, then, is divided from the married woman in her life and her whole character, she will recognize in everything the works that befit a virgin. She will keep the beauty of virginity uncorrupted in every deed, so as not to pour herself out indiscriminately on unbecoming things and spoil by what she does the very thing she is striving to pursue.

22. In this way, then, the true virgin will be exact in speaking, in keeping silent and in going out. But, as I said, she must go out not casually or at random, nor alone, but in keeping with the aim stated earlier, in the company of women decorous in life and in age. She must never be seen in unseemly alleys or in marketplaces where disorderly people happen to gather. Rather, choosing her time for going out well, she should appear to those she meets such in bearing, in gait and in every movement that all who encounter her look on her as on a statue of God. They are struck to reverence at the sight, their minds are sobered by the reminder of the good, they revere what they see, and as… [(84) "In the first place": [?] the Paris edition reads ὅλως, "at all."]
…give way, as I said, to the image of God, and [?] [?] [Manuscripts: "beholding … they moved." Edition: "being moved." … "by all those in." The Venetian edition has "of all those."]

…has a [?] place of punishment. Since out of chastity she can choose nothing else, neither her husband's death, because of the bitterness of widowhood, nor his life, because living with him is so unpleasant, her soul is constantly cut to pieces with griefs by a misery she cannot escape. Then she bears children. Either she sees them turn out good, and all her life carries the grief of losing them, greater than the pangs of their birth; or she sees them turn out bad, and bears a reproach for having had children heavier than that of childlessness. Or, before she has come to experience the evils just mentioned, she has become bride and widow at once. The childless woman brought down to widowhood is neither wife nor virgin nor mother. Having fallen at once from all the supposed pleasures of marriage, she has lost the beauty of virginity for a brief pleasure, and has experienced marriage only enough to learn the bitterness of widowhood. Or, raising her children as orphans in her widowhood, she sees them as a reminder of her grief for her husband. She is always in tears, always groaning, always mired in distress over bringing them up. Not only does she have no consolation to balance the misfortune that has befallen her, but she lies exposed as pitiable plunder to relatives and servants and her children's guardians, often even to the children themselves once they are grown, and in short to anyone who wishes to mistreat her. She brings nothing into the world but her own life as a drama of grief and mourning. And—why say more?—the woman who buys her husband as a master with a dowry is a slave instead of a free woman. For the small pleasure of marriage she has sold off her natural freedom, and opened marriage for herself as a door to untold pangs and a whole occasion of pains. For the curse remains unbroken against her, sung at every marriage like a wedding song: "In sorrow you shall bear children, and your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you." But the virgin, having broken the yoke of a husband and run wholly to the Lord, has broken along with the yoke the pain that comes from the curse. She has fled the pangs of bearing children, fled slavery to a mortal husband, and in short all the terrors of marriage. Along with the rest she has also escaped the intricate nets that lead to the abundant sin of this present life. Above all, she has fled first of all the corruption that comes from the union of flesh, and so, wholly incorrupt in a fleshless soul, she is wedded to the Lord. She no longer allows her turning to be toward a mortal husband, but shows herself self-sufficient to the Lord in a well-ordered life. For she saw that the basis of marriage is corruption and outrage, and from that basis she wisely reckoned up the whole drama of marriage. Having escaped the first cause of its miseries, she escaped along with it the evil that grows from that cause. Therefore "the unmarried woman cares for the things of the…

…of the Lord, how to please the Lord; but she who has married cares for the things of the world, how to please her husband. And the wife and the virgin are divided. The unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and in spirit.

24. So in dividing the care between herself and the woman who cares for the things of the world, she has thrown onto the one yoked to a perishable husband the worldly concerns for perishable things, and has taken upon herself the concerns for imperishable things, which are akin to her own bridegroom. That is why she is found caring for none of the things of the world: so that she may not seem to share her care with the other woman. Instead, purely cleansed of all worldly concerns, she has turned to the bridegroom with a pure and untroubled mind. She does not distrust the providing power of her own husband, and so she is not troubled about necessities as that other woman is. Rather, trusting both in his love for her and in his power, which suffices for all things, she takes thought for nothing else than how to please him, and by that very thought of how to please him she draws his goodwill toward her still further.

What is it for a virgin to please God, if not to show her natural beauty always shining with the virtues through ascetic discipline, and to keep it wholly incorrupt? So to wish to please God is nothing other than to make oneself praiseworthy, blessed and like him. And so the woman who cares how to please the Lord turns out to be bringing no gain through her care to the one she cares to please. Rather, through her care for him she gathers beauty and incorruption for herself. If, then, the virgin's [?] is so great, and through caring how to please the Lord she benefits herself entirely and makes herself blessed, she must never be found caring for the things of the world. For when she cares for the things of the world she must necessarily neglect her care for the Lord as well, and convict herself of distrusting her guardian. It is not possible both to trust him as able to supply everything and to be anxious and agitated over worldly concerns. But if she cares how to please the Lord, she must surely know that he too cares how to please her, though he is in no way obliged to. For if a woman who has made a mortal man the protector of her life receives from him, in return for her care for him, his care in everything, much more will she who has entrusted her protection to God and chosen to live with him receive from him, who provides for all things, a return more abundant than her care for him. You have a pledge for this trust in the care he has already shown. For if he took thought for her when she was not yet caring to please him, and readily gave himself up for her so that he might sanctify her with his own blood, much more will he take thought for her when she wishes to please him. Together with everything else that leads to true life, he will also take upon himself the outward things that are needed along with it.

(5) Needed along with it: two manuscripts read "needed." [?]

25. Yet she will not seek to be pampered by the Lord beyond what is pressing need, demanding superfluities like a pleasure-loving wife. It is not fitting for him to give things that hinder her pleasing him by turning her toward the pleasures of the body, nor is it good for her to receive things that unsettle her mind and distract it from pleasing him. Instead, having wisely set the necessities of bodily life as the limit of her need, she will ask for nothing more. And when she is pressed by want of necessities, as often happens to test her love for him, she will not grieve faint-heartedly. Bearing all things, hoping all things, enduring all things, fastened to him with unfeigned love, she will feast without distraction on his beauty, her soul dwelling in an outward body that is, in a sense, dead and without feeling.

Think of a man in love with a passing beauty. He not only spends his money and all his wealth unsparingly on his passion, but despises food and sleep, clothing and appearance and all reputation, and even his own body and the life in it, for the sole sake of winning his love. He boldly leaps over walls and houses and everything in between, and rushes like a madman against swords. If he would fail by going to his love in his usual way, he cares nothing about it; if he must disguise himself and creep in an unseemly guise to win her, he gladly puts up with it. In the same way, the one who truly loves God and cares how to please the beloved ought to despise not only money and wealth, so as to assure the beloved of his love by obeying the commands of his precepts, but also necessary food and sleep, outward appearance, and the reputation of this world, which is truly corrupt. Disregarding even his own body and the life in it in order to win the heavenly love, he ought to leap over the walls of blood relations, the houses of fathers, and the world in between, and to spring against the swords of martyrdom if they meet him. If he would not win his love by living in his usual guise, he ought gladly to put up with a poor guise and a life the many reproach, so that, maddened lawfully with a divine madness, so to speak, for the enjoyment of the good, he may enjoy the one who is truly lovely as much as he wishes. Calling this lover to himself out of earthly passions, the beloved said: "Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house, and come into the land that I will show you." And he followed eagerly, as though he saw what he longed for, and for the sake of his love he…

…gladly endured wandering, saying: "Who will separate us from the love of God? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?" For he knew that whoever loves father or mother more than what is truly good is not worthy to enjoy it, and that whoever does not renounce all his possessions, and even his own life, is not worthy to be called a friend and lover of the Lord. That is why those who care only for his things, wishing to show how genuine their devotion to him is, say: "Look, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?" And proclaiming to them already from that moment a worthy reward for their love of him, he says: "Truly, truly I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses, or fields, or brothers, or sisters, or wife, or children for the sake of my name will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life." For it was only right that those who had shown by their deeds, throughout their whole life, that their love for him was pure should receive rewards worthy of the sweat they had shed for him.

26. The virgin who loves with such a love must despise luxury and wealth and what the world counts as delight. Trampling on passing glory and vanity and bodily beauty and passionate flatteries, she must follow the Lord without turning back, saying: "But for me it is good to cling to God, to put my hope in the Lord." Whatever those infatuated with this life count as good, whatever name one cares to give it, she must declare ridiculous and shameful. She must see only one good, her own, and tend it with her eyes fixed upon it. For the bridegroom repays her for her love of him: even if she is a slave, low-born, poor and obscure, even if she is an outcast in earthly life, he ennobles her through her union with himself and makes her a queen of the heavens. He not only honors her nature with the nobility of incorruption, but also adorns her lavishly and in many ways with outward clothing, as his own bride. Marveling at her glory, the Psalmist says to the bridegroom: "The queen stood at your right hand in clothing…"

…to repay the one who died for her with her own incorruption, but to live wantonly, be pampered and conform to the world, and not to share poverty and lowliness in her way of life with him who became poor for her. Yet she should do so, so that when he returns to his own wealth of divinity, she who shared poverty with him who became poor for her may be found a partner in his wealth and in his kingdom in heaven. Let her therefore pass by everything that appears to sight, even if to some it seems to carry an appearance of beauty; or rather, let her not even deign to look at it in the first place. Let her undergo a divine ecstasy like the one experienced by him who said in his ecstasy, "Every man is a liar," and, standing outside the senses, and outside her fellow servants by means of them, let her feast, with a naked mind I say, on her own love. Let her never direct a glance, a movement or a word passionately toward anyone, but make all her powers handmaids of her own bridegroom. For he who sees everywhere examines her inner disposition most precisely through everything.

27. The virgin must not commit adultery in any part, not with the tongue, nor the ear, nor the eye, nor touch, nor any other sense at all, and still less with the mind. Rather, she must keep her body ready like a temple or bridal chamber [?] for the bridegroom, and in it lay her soul to rest as a pure bride. For he scrutinizes not only what human eyes see, but also what lies hidden in the mind, and no woman committing adultery could escape his eye. Women who live with mortal husbands, when they have run aground on wickedness and busy themselves with the business of adultery, watch their husbands' comings and goings, guard against their eyes and ears with all possible cunning, steal a hidden adulterous word and glance, and glut their hearing and sight with licentious pleasure. But she who is betrothed to the Lord cannot escape his sight, his hearing or his presence, and does everything in his sight. Therefore the virgin, even if she says something when alone, must know that she is speaking in the bridegroom's hearing; even if she does something alone, she must not be unaware that he sees it precisely; even if she thinks something, she must be convinced that he keenly observes it as it stirs in her heart. "Will anyone do something in secret," it says, "and I not see it?" And: "He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, will he not perceive? He who instructs the nations, will he not rebuke? He who teaches man knowledge"—how will he not know all things, when all things are naked and laid bare before his eyes? That is why the man of sin, his mind blinded by his own wickedness and deceiving himself…

…may say as he likes: "Darkness covers me, and the walls around me, and who sees me?" Let the bride, then, test her own glance against the Lord's gaze: if he is pleased as he sees it, let her move it with confidence for that very reason. But if it does not please him, let her not deceive herself into thinking that because no human being sees, he too fails to notice. Let her examine in the same way her word, her thought, and the movement of each of her limbs and fingers. If he is pleased with these, let her proceed with each; if not, let her feel shame [?] as before one who sees. For if she cares how to please the Lord, she must do nothing that does not please him.

28. If she dares a nod or a word because no human being sees, she is first and foremost her own accuser right there, since she carries within her the very intention of escaping notice as the accuser of a bad conscience. Then she is plainly shown to be blind to the dignity of the bridegroom. For he is incorporeal, and stands in the midst of whispers and glances and thoughts. He turns away from such a woman's deceitful intent and shows her to be hateful for the reputation of virginity she displays to outsiders. For by deceiving human eyes, as though she were betrothed to him for life, she is neither his bride nor purely a man's wife. Instead, she steals human glory for her virginity through the virginal habit, and parades her virginity before men under the very eyes of the bridegroom…

…not enduring what is worthy of the bridegroom. For even if no other human being is present, the virgin is present to herself, and she ought to feel shame before herself more than before anyone. She will not guard her conduct before others as worthy of respect and then dishonor herself as unworthy of it. Rather, as I said, she will feel shame first before herself and her own conscience, even when she is entirely alone, and then before the guardian angel who stands beside her. For "their angels," it says, "always behold the face of your Father who is in heaven." While hiding from human sight, she must not despise the angel entrusted with the care of our salvation; above all the virgin, who has this angel as the escort of her bridal virginity, as it were, and its guardian. And even before the angels, let her feel shame before the bridegroom himself, who is present everywhere, and his Father, and the Holy Spirit. But why go through them one by one? There are the countless multitudes of angels, and with them the holy spirits of the fathers. There is not one of these who does not see everywhere: unseen by bodily eyes, they take in everything with an incorporeal gaze and know it all. So by this reasoning too, if the virgin wishes to escape the notice of the many, she will naturally feel shame before these, who are so many and so great, far more than before human beings. And since she chose to hide her sin from the multitude, but it is impossible to escape these, who are a multitude, she would never do anything improper. By reflecting on such things about herself in the present life, she will, I think, secure herself on every side.

30. Remembering that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, she will be afraid not only to do anything shameful, but even to think it. For our mind is like a painter, and shapes thoughts on the soul as on a tablet, however it likes. It is unseen, and free because of its self-determination; since it is incorporeal, it is never cramped in its eager painting, but finds as much room as it wants and inscribes, I say, whatever it wishes with its thoughts. A painter fills a tablet with a varied scene somewhere behind a screen, then suddenly brings it out into the open, removes the outer coverings and sets it up publicly for the many to view. He no longer acts as interpreter of what he has painted, but lets all the viewers, then and in time to come, study the painting as it is. In the same way the mind, after its departure from this life, when the body has been taken away from it like a covering over the tablet of the soul that it painted with its thoughts throughout life, [brings] into the light what was painted in secret…
