[APPENDIX TO THE WORKS] […] and shows it to all. Then the tablet of the soul can be seen, full of varied scenes and laid out for all to view. If divine scenes drawn from sacred readings and virtue-loving thoughts are seen inscribed on it, then the mind that painted it, and the tablet of the soul that received the painting, are judged worthy of all praise. Those examining the painting will not want to leave the sight, so worth seeing is it. All will admire the beauty and outline of each thing painted, and indeed the godlike form of what is inscribed, and will call that divine painter blessed for using his life in the flesh well. Beneath this covering of the body, night and day, he engraved such paintings on the tablet of his soul with a hand that loved beauty, beyond anything the viewers had expected.

But if the paintings turn out to be shameful and unseemly, the painter will be seen by all to deserve shame and laughter. Perhaps before the tablet of his soul was laid bare he held out other hopes, but once the veil of the body was removed he showed the viewers everything contrary to what they had hoped. Where then will he hide, when he is judged by all in comparison with the other? His thoughts will accuse or else defend one another among themselves. And where will that tablet of the soul be put away, after filling the viewers' eyes with shameful scenes and every monstrous form? Consider those who have blemishes on their bodies. Before they are stripped, they keep them hidden by their clothing and unknown to the many, and often, adorned in the most splendid clothes, they are even suspected of being handsome underneath because of their outward finery. But once they have taken off their clothes and been seen naked in a bath, they appear ridiculous, and show a body that, contrary to their great outward reputation, is disfigured by countless blemishes. Once the body has been seen naked by all, there is no need to explain where or how it is blemished: the moment it is stripped, the blemish seen on each limb explains itself to the eye. So too, when we have taken off the veil of the flesh, we will be able neither to cover nor in any way to hide the blemishes in our soul. Seen in the sight of all, we shall show naked to every eye what we secretly had and kept hidden in the body as in a garment. There will no longer be any room for denial or excuses, when the deeds themselves are seen and, once seen, are recognized in the one who did them.

…and from where he slipped in and laid hands on another man's wife, and how the woman gave herself to him for the lawless act. As on a tablet, I say, every detail will be seen precisely inscribed, and not only the deeds already done, but also, where the deeds did not go forward, the thoughts that arose on the tablet of the soul. For a painting in the soul is nothing other than a thought about something impressed upon it; and an imaginative and elaborate thought in the soul is nothing other than a painting inscribed with the colors and sizes, and also the shapes, of imagination, which the mind has painted upon it.

Consider someone who has learned the art of shorthand. He carries impressed on his soul the shapes and names of all the signs, and also the forms of the groups of eight and of four [?]. As dictation requires, he shows on the tablet with his hand what is inscribed in his soul by memory. Some signs he has shown by marking them with the stylus, while others, not yet shown by hand, nevertheless lie stored and written down in his soul. So too the soul has carried some thoughts into action by working through the body, while others, which it did not get as far as accomplishing in the body and displaying to us, it keeps impressed within itself. It accomplishes these, if not bodily, then incorporeally within itself by its own proper activity. For as it is the body's work to accomplish something bodily, so it is the soul's work to bring to completion with its thoughts whatever imaginings please it, as it wishes. That is why sins of thought too are justly judged, not simply as imaginings, but as deeds done in the soul.

Even if the hand does not write the signs, the whole soul is nevertheless written over everywhere with their shapes, and anyone who stripped off the body would see it entirely written over with what is called the "commentary" [?]. In the same way, after we strip off the body, every thought will be seen written on the soul as in a painting. And just as someone who has not learned the signs does not have their forms inscribed in his soul, while someone who has learned them, even if his hand does not write, has recorded their forms in his soul by learning them, so too someone who has never thought of a particular sin does not have its image written in his soul. But whoever has thought of it, even if the deed did not go forward, still has the images of what he thought in his soul, clearly written as on a tablet. Yet in the one case, the person who learned the signs might, by neglecting to write them out, lose them from memory through forgetfulness, so that in time he could no longer call to mind the shape, form or name of any "eight." So too the person who has thought improper things, if he neglects those thoughts and occupies his mind with other, better ones, might in time cast them out of his memory and wipe them off the tablet of the soul through forgetfulness. For memory is nothing other than an impression of thoughts, as it were in the soul, an underpainting. And how [?]… For there is nothing in the [?]…

…is it possible to escape the accounting for those thoughts whose memory, still stirring in the soul, displays their images alive on the tablet to those who look? So then, so that the tablet of our soul may not be seen to be full of shameful things, let us wipe out by forgetting the memories of base thoughts, and in their place let us imprint the memories of good ones. Then we, who are now hidden by the covering of the body, will not, once we have laid it aside, be seen by all as shameful because of our blemishes and disgraceful because of what is written there, contrary to the reputation we hold in the present life. 32. For perhaps this is what the Apostle meant: "The sins of some people are evident, going before them to judgment; but for others they follow after." The sins that are evident to all people, by which they have wickedly caused those who saw them to stumble into blasphemy and into similar deeds, go before them. But those that are hidden from people and done in secret do not stay behind just because people are unaware of them. They follow after them inseparably, so that, by revealing both themselves and the man who did them and escaped the notice of the many, they may hand him over both to the people who did not know and to the just judgment. So the wretch is caught between his own evils: dragged to judgment by the evident ones that go before him, and driven on by the hidden ones that follow him inseparably. And explaining this thought, he goes on to say: "Likewise also good works"—those that shine before people, so that when they see them they may glorify our Father in heaven—"are evident, and those that are otherwise cannot remain hidden." For we who are now unknown must be made manifest, as to what sort of deeds we belong to, before the judgment seat of Christ, "who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. And then each one will receive praise from God," when each of us receives what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad. 33. We must not, then, pass over in silence the other meaning either, which is able to anoint the prudent virgin more nobly for the contests that lie before her. Consider the wonderful Paul. While he was still in the body, some of his works went before him: many of those brought to perfection through his teaching and way of life had gone ahead of him to the life there, and had prepared for him with God, the just judge, the rewards for the sweat he poured out on their behalf. Other works have followed him, now that he has departed and is with Christ, right up to the present, as those who are trained in virtue through him by the sacred writings of his letters send from here their praises, and with them his rewards, to that good teacher. So too, in the opposite case,

some sins go before: the sins of those who were harmed by wicked words or deeds and have gone ahead into Hades, where they are preparing punishments for those who caused the harm. And other sins follow after: when, even after such people's death, others are harmed by them through the vice they left behind in the world. For just as the blessed David to this day benefits people toward godliness and the knowledge of providence, and those who are benefited by him send from here voices of praise that follow after him for his own good deeds, so Marcion and the rest of those who sowed heretical doctrines in the world do harm. All those who are harmed by them here hand over the ones who began the wickedness, though they died long ago, to ever more bitter punishments there. For if, he says, anyone who causes one of the little ones to stumble is judged worthy of such a death, then the one who causes stumbling by having left behind, through his wicked life, so many examples for the corruption of morals, or by having brought forth doctrines that destroy souls, would rightly and justly be declared liable, even after his own death, for all the deaths of those who die because of him. For each person wounded or killed here because of him, the one responsible is wounded and dies in the age there. And if in this way too some deeds go before and others follow after, and just as those that follow from vice hand over the one responsible to greater punishment for each person harmed, so those that follow from virtue count the teacher worthy of greater rewards for each person benefited and turned away from vice, then the virgin too has, in each case, whether of virtue or of vice, some deeds that go before and others that follow after. Wretched is she who, besides the punishment for her own sin, is handed over to ever more bitter punishment because of the fall of others to whom she showed the slippery paths to sin. But thrice-blessed is she who, besides her own crowns, is crowned also because of those who are crowned through their zeal to imitate her, every day, even after death, in the age there. 34. If, then, nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, then for all the reasons already given the virgin, even when she is alone, will take care to remain without sin, showing respect not only for the eyes of other people but, much more, I say, for her own eyes and for those of the angels who see everywhere. "For this reason," he says, "a woman ought to have authority on her head, because of the angels." For the virgin must not, even if she is sitting alone by herself at home, carelessly uncover herself because no human being is present. For the nature of the female, I say, is very alluring, enough to draw all male nature toward itself. And it is not only for this reason that she should guard against the assaults of the demons, always suspecting them as they lie in wait for us unseen; she ought to have authority also, he says, because of the angels, who are revered by all. For a man, as one who is in some way of angelic dignity, [?] [Editor's notes: for τοῦ read τό. For ἀναφυέναι perhaps read ἀναφανῆναι.]

may let himself be seen with bare head, confident before the brethren. But let a woman, who has received a nature far inferior to a man's, have authority on her head, and by having authority on her head let her decorously acknowledge her subjection to the one who is superior. For this reason, he says, nature itself has covered their head from above with hair, teaching by this very fact that a woman should never carelessly uncover, I will not say any other part of her body, but not even her head. And since women sometimes grow bold enough to do this when they are alone and no men are present, he added a dignity more to be revered than that of men, saying "because of the angels," who are present everywhere and see what is done. Let every woman, then, and the virgin still more, revere the angels, even when she is the only human being in the house. And when she has of necessity to attend to her body, let her keep her head and every other part covered and hurry through the task. As far as possible, let her conceal her limbs, revering not only her own eyes, and with them always the eyes of the angels, but also, as if in her own place of ascetic training, [training] herself diligently in modesty [?]

35. And if she will not carelessly strip even when she is by herself, much more, when brothers in Christ are present, will she adorn herself soberly with both tunic and modesty. She will not simply refrain from letting any of the limbs that ought to be covered by clothing be partly exposed; she will cover herself with the greatest care, so as to cause no harm. In this way not only will she herself remain safe from assault, but those who see her will take no occasion of harm from the sight. "For the sons of God," he says, "seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, came down to them." Beauty partly exposed is enough to bewitch even sons of God into pleasure, and to show them to be mortal, like men who die because of it. Therefore she must not care only for her own safety and despise the salvation of those who might be harmed. She must keep the beauty of her virginity inviolate on every side, also as far as she herself is concerned [?], and procure for those who see her the gain of life, not the death of sin. For even if she trusts that her virginity cannot fall, she must still take care, he says, not to put a stumbling block or an occasion of offense in her brother's way. 36. Thus the virgin, being soundly disposed in mind and movement, in form and bearing, both alone and with others, toward what pleases her bridegroom, [?] [Editor's notes: 42 αὐτόθι: some manuscripts read αὐτόθεν. 43 προστέθεικε: the printed editions add τῶν ἀγγέλων, which [?]. The printed editions read: ἀεὶ … καλύπτουσα.]

[?] having painted an image of God [from head to] foot [?], we skillfully bring her forward in this way to those of the household of faith, so that, seen truly as the Lord's bride in both bearing and speech, she may benefit those who converse with her. Let her converse, then, as a bride, with modesty, with the servants of the bridegroom, I say, and let her keep her sobriety everywhere as she converses. For she must be innocent as a dove, but prudent as the serpent. Souls in bodies cannot converse with one another nakedly about virtue. They are compelled to use the bodies that surround them as instruments for both voice and sight. Someone who cannot see the beauty of a soul bound to a body, or hear it in speech [?], sees the movement of the body in which it is, and by listening to the voice that comes through the body he infers the soul's beauty from these. And not only the voice or a glance shows the form of the soul as in a mirror; "a man's attire, and his laughter, and his gait" also "tell what he is." But some people, from listening with pleasure to a musician, have little by little and without noticing come to love no longer the musician but the visible instrument through which they enjoy the musician's skill. For this reason the virgin must of necessity guard her hearing and her eye carefully, lest she unawares come to love, instead of the speaking soul, the thing through which it speaks. For there is one who envies our disposition toward the good, and who tries by every means to take away what we long for and craftily substitute his own in place of the object of our desire. This is how some, from listening with pleasure to the discourse on virtue and from being devoted to the soul that moved it, were caught unawares. Through continual hearing and seeing they had the shape of the bodily features stamped on them, and their hearing was strangely charmed by the voice. In the end they no longer loved the soul that produced the discourse through the voice, for whose sake they had earlier cherished the person, but the body that ministered to them the good things of the soul. For even the Greeks say that vices live next door to virtues. Beside each door of virtue, on either side, he has fitted a vice of the most similar appearance. So one who is zealous for virtue stands first at its door and thinks he is knocking on it. When one of the doors of vice, on this side or that, is opened to him, he is deceived by the resemblance and goes in as if into the house of virtue. Then, laughed at by all for being deceived, he may learn with time and experience that he is not only far from the virtue whose door he once thought he was knocking at, but has never crossed its threshold at all, and has not even, as he previously thought, stood at its door and knocked. In this way he has deceived those who wish to be courageous for virtue and shown them to be rash, and those who fear the reproaches that fall on

rashness he has exposed as cowardly and faint-hearted. Those who are eager to be compassionate he has wrongly made soft toward the passions, and those who flee from passion he has made pitiless and inhuman. So too, those who pursue the beauty of love he has either hurled, unbecomingly, by a falsely named love, into the pleasures of the flesh and a life that all condemn, or, as they guard against blame in these matters, he has made them haters of their brothers and insensible to the good. Again, then: "Do not turn aside to the right or to the left," lest you go astray and slip through one of the doors of vice. Walk the middle road of virtue, looking everywhere at how carefully you walk, not as unwise but as wise, for you walk in the midst of snares and pass along the battlements of cities. Take care that you never carelessly set your foot in a snare, nor fall from the wall of our city and die miserably. 37. One must, then, love those who urge one toward the bridegroom, but one must keep that love just and not confused. Otherwise she may, from continually hearing them speak about the bridegroom, one day come to love the bridegroom's servants as much as the bridegroom himself. She would then both lower the bridegroom's dignity and do the greatest wrong to those who lead the bride to him, by treating them as equal in honor to the Master. Already some women have unawares come to love the servants impiously, not as much as the bridegroom but even more. They have altogether forgotten the bridegroom to whom they were once betrothed and have become wholly the brides of the bridegroom's household servants—or rather not even of the bridegroom's servants, but have been found to be the shameful wives of strangers. For our bridegroom is found to have no fleshly servant; all his servants live by the Spirit. So those women who have strangely married themselves not to the spirit of those who serve the bridegroom but to their flesh have clearly shown both that those men are strangers to the bridegroom's service, and that they themselves are married not to the bridegroom's servants but to the slaves of another. Let them, therefore, converse carefully with these men too, wisely cutting off the bodily familiarity that secretly grows out of conversation. Let them be on their guard as they converse, lest, from confidence that these men belong to the bridegroom's household, they unawares either trip those men up into what they should not do, or strangely cast themselves down, contrary to the goal set before them, into the pleasures of the flesh. One must indeed have love for one's neighbors, since "You shall love your neighbor as yourself"; and the bridegroom gave the bride this command because it pleased him. He says, "You shall love," and "inasmuch as you do it to one of these, you do it to me," your bridegroom. But love must not be passionate, nor falsely bear the name of love while in practice destroying the worth of true love. For as long as

you are seen to love the brothers because of your love for the bridegroom, you preserve the dignity of love both toward him and toward them. But when you love them no longer for his sake but for their own, out of familiarity, you corrupt your love toward him as well and make it passionate, and then you have a falsely named love and not the true one. For love does not touch the passions of the flesh. Nor is it irrational, bringing its dignity down indiscriminately onto bodies out of animal habit. It is rational and wholly full of wisdom, and wisely weighs itself out justly according to the worth of each person. She honors the bridegroom's servants with reasoned regard for his sake, but she cherishes him not for their sake, because they talk with her about him, but for his own. If anyone loves him, she regards that person as a companion because of his affection for the bridegroom. But if anyone neglects love for him, she no longer regards that person as one of her own, even if he flatters her; rather, the flattery itself makes her suspect a plot. Such a man neglects the bridegroom she is so taken with, yet entices her with a feigned devotion to her bridegroom, as though he were laboring with her to please him, while he strives through constant conversation to transfer her love to himself. Under the name and guise of a groomsman he craftily becomes the bride's adulterer. This is how many women, under the name of love, have been carried down little by little through familiarity to the passions of the flesh, and have been exposed as harlots and adulteresses, strangers not only to marriage with the Lord but even to marriage that is lawful according to the flesh among human beings. For having promised virginity to the Lord and then been overcome by the pleasures of the flesh, they want to cloak the sin of fornication under the name of marriage. They are not unaware, I think, even if they pretend ignorance, that a woman who has broken the pledges she gave her bridegroom is neither the bride of the one she lawlessly abandoned, nor can she be found to be the lawful wife of the man to whom she joined herself through passion. 38. For marriage is lawful and in accordance with the divine Scriptures when the passion of pleasure does not get ahead of the use for which the law exists, but reason sets out the purpose of marriage, namely necessary help and the succession of children, and so betroths a marriage that is truly honorable. When reason has first secured the necessary ends of marriage, and a holy foundation has been laid lawfully in the Lord, then the pleasure of union, which follows from what is necessary in marriage, is found to make the two one flesh. For since reason in the soul first took hold of the souls and joined them according to evident necessity, it is fitting that the lawful union of the bodies in which they dwell should follow upon their prior union. But when the souls have set before themselves some other starting point, and the bodies, having pursued their own ends for the sake of pleasure, unite the souls within them [Editor's note: 55 "feigned devotion": Latin adscita; Cotelier [?].]

as slaves to the passion that matches them, then the souls, becoming a mere consequence of the evils of the flesh, bring about an unlawful union. For a deed that the reason and law in the soul did not lead is denounced by conscience as altogether lawless. That is why he says, "A wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes"—not without condition, but "only in the Lord," he says. For even a woman whom her husband's death has set free for marriage ought to marry not merely because she has been set free, but in the Lord. And what does it mean for a marriage to be contracted in the Lord? It means not being dragged into union beforehand by the pleasures of the flesh, but choosing marriage by judging what is profitable for life. That is why the Maker also [arranged] in nature what is necessary for marriage [?]

39. If this is how things stand, let the woman who has been carried down from virginity to the passions of the flesh not deceive herself, I say, into thinking that marriage will be counted to her in place of the sin. First, because she has laid pleasure down as a bad foundation for the union, and with it the sin of transgression for herself. Then, because she is not free (her husband has not died, that she might marry whom she wishes), she will be called an adulteress while her immortal husband lives, since she brings a mortal into the Lord's bridal chamber because of the passions of the flesh. That the bridegroom had first secured the lawful rights of marriage is witnessed before all by the habit of virginity, by the pledges, and by her appearances in public in his honor, for she took pride in him as her husband and paraded in public as belonging to the husband who had first claimed her. For a virgin does not go out from her father's chambers until she has been joined to a lawful husband and enrolled under him as the master and protector of her life, and then she goes out from her father's house under the name of the husband she has obtained. So too this virgin went out from her father's chambers as one who had enrolled the bridegroom as her lawful husband, and she makes her public appearances under his protection. And if those who see these appearances are witnesses of them, then the same people are also witnesses of whom she was joined to, or what husband she had enrolled, when she came out of her father's house into public. And if this marriage is manifest to the witnesses, through her public appearances, and to all, and her husband, I say, has not died, then such a woman commits adultery while her husband lives [?], committing adultery for life. Or rather, she fornicates by enjoying licentious pleasure, and she commits adultery unlawfully because her husband is alive. And I do not see how she, instead of the immortal God, can cherish a mortal man to her own harm, acting impiously against her husband before his very eyes by her lawless unions; nor how that man madly dared [to defile] [?] the Lord's bed. For from human affairs one must [judge] the penalty of those who sin in this way [?] … is called an adulteress.

…to consider. What does she deserve who, instead of (59) a noble husband, corrupts herself with her own slave and brings the servant into her master's bed to plot against him? And what does the slave deserve who wantonly throws himself on his own mistress and his lord's bed? 40. Yet these wise women, having dared such impiety against themselves because of the passions of the flesh, not only fail to weep over it, though they could prepare for themselves a lighter place by their tears, but go on to deny even the virginity they once promised. They know that breaking virginity is shameful and disgraceful in everyone's eyes, because it is slavery to pleasure. So they think they can soothe the sin by denying it, which is the greater evil. These admirable women feel shame (60) before men, to whom they offer their denial as a defence for their transgression. But they no longer fear the Lord, to whom they gave their right hands, because they have fallen into the depths of evil. They do not realize that they are absurdly building up a double charge against themselves, before men and before the Lord. Men know the virginity that was publicly proclaimed, even if these women deny having promised it, and they turn away from, and even hate, the frenzy and brazenness of denying what everyone acknowledges. The Lord, besides their breaking of the covenant of virginity, judges more bitterly at his tribunal the denial they offer in place of repentance. So that the virgin may not fall into this pit of sin under the name of love, let her pursue a love that is pure and free of passion. For once she has slipped (61) into pleasure, the mask of marriage will have no place for her. Nor will she be able to deceive, under the name of marriage, her living Husband, who has not released her, after impiously preferring a mortal man to him for an act of adultery, despite all the honours he gave her. It would not be out of place to apply to such women the apostle's words: 'When they grow wanton against Christ, they want to marry, and so incur condemnation for having set aside their first faith.' What they are wickedly contriving is not marriage but lifelong adultery. 41. Let no servant, then, be driven by such a frenzy of impiety as to lay hands on his master's bride. Let no temple-robber be so mad as to touch the undefiled priestess with licentious hands. Let no one sink to such folly that, seeing how great a penalty hangs over temple-robbers, he profanely seizes with a robber's hand not lifeless vessels made of gold and silver but living, breathing offerings themselves. Or rather, let no one be so unholy as to burn up barbarously with the torches of licentiousness not the lifeless vessels in the temple but the very temple of the Lord, that is, the virgin's body, and the most precious thing of all within it, the virgin's soul, the holiest offering in the temple of the Lord. (59) Ἡ ἀντί: two manuscripts read εἴη ἀντί. (60) Αἰδούμεναι: four manuscripts read αἱρούμεναι.

[?] But if the virgin has given herself up willingly, breaking her covenant with the Bridegroom, and for the pleasure of passion has thrown everything into confusion and trampled on it all together, temple, offering, her friendship with him and her share in the kingdom, do not lend yourself to such a woman as a partner in sin. Even the good Joseph refused to lend himself to his mistress, who was mad for him, so that she could enjoy her licentiousness. 'But if you do not enter into marriage with her, she will give herself to another.' Then let that man answer for his own sin, and keep yourself clear of answering for a share in the transgression against the Lord. 'The Son of Man must be handed over,' it says, 'but woe to the one through whom the Son of Man is handed over; it would have been better for him if he had not been born.' Would he not judge [?] in the same way the woman who once promised virginity but has changed her mind (62) and yoked herself to some man to enjoy pleasure? Even if she says, 'I must marry, just as the Son of Man must be handed over,' still, woe to the man through whom she breaks her covenant with the Bridegroom and fulfils her desire! For it would have been better for that man (I dare say it) to suffer the same fate (63) than to be found condemned as a partner in that licentious woman's transgression against the Lord. Do you not hear that 'he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery'? For even if she has been divorced for a cause, it says, her husband is still alive. 42. Why, then, do you trouble the divorced woman? Why do you not give her time to correct the faults for which she was divorced, so that the one who divorced her, moved with compassion once she has been corrected (64), may take his own member back to himself? Instead, you snatch away the time for correction by marrying the divorced woman while her husband is alive. 'Let her,' it says, 'either return to the living man and be taken back as a better wife, or remain forever neither widow nor wife, paying the penalty for the cause of divorce she gave her husband.' But before she has even understood her own sin in the divorce, you snatch her into union with you and absurdly make her bolder toward sin. As long as the husband lives, you are continually committing adultery with another man's wife, and, as I said, you absurdly make her careless about faults in married life. [Notes:] [?] … ἔκρινεν. [?] … διορθώσει.

…Bridegroom. For if Christ is light, resurrection, incorruption, life and all the other good things given to us from the Father, then what has the wretched woman who released herself from Christ done but release herself from light into darkness, from life into death, from incorruption into corruption, and from resurrection into the terrible fall of Hades and death? If she considers these things and how deep an abyss of evils this is, she will surely shudder at the gloom of sin, full of confusion and dejection, and will long all the more for the sweetness of the light in which she once lived. When she sees how fearful death is and how hideous corruption, she will leap away from them all the more eagerly toward life and immortality. When she peers into the most grievous fall of Hades, she will surely cling more warmly to the resurrection granted (65) her by the Lord. For she is surely not so full of madness that, once her passion has died down with time, she would still prefer the mortal bridegroom to the immortal one. Why, then, do you [?] the wretched woman's slip? Why do you snatch away the time she needs to reflect on her sin? Why do you shut out (66) the time for deliberation, so that by marrying a woman whom the Lord has not released you [?] yourself not a husband [?]… 43. Let the virgin, then, be untouched by any hand, since she is a most eminent offering to God. Keeping herself undefiled in body and thought, let her associate safely, I say, even with her brothers in Christ. The genuine servant of God carefully directs her to this when he says: 'I want you all to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil.' And: 'I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts may be corrupted and led away from your simple devotion to Christ.' Above all, then, the virgin's thoughts must be kept entirely uncorrupted. For while the soul remains uncorrupted, the body too is kept uncorrupted. But when the soul has been corrupted by wicked thoughts, then even if the body seems to remain uncorrupted, its incorruption is not found pure, since it is being corrupted by the defilement of the thoughts. We must love, then, but must measure the amount of our love with reason and prudent judgment (67). For 'love does not behave unbecomingly'; and, 'Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.' It is absurd for someone who is eager to be free to entangle himself, under the name of love, in the bonds of pleasure through familiarity, so that he can no longer be free in body or in soul, as he promised. For the soul of such a person is not free, since it is busy with the passions of an animal familiarity (68), nor is the body… (65) Δεδωρημένης: the Colbert manuscript reads δεδομένης. (66) Ἐκκλείεις: one manuscript reads ἐκλύεις. (67) Μετροῦντας: the editions [?] read μετροῦντος.

44. By this we do not discourage anyone from loving the brothers. On the contrary, we allow them to love everyone as if they had been born of the same womb, but we advise that even those born of the same womb be loved with caution. For there is a danger that sin may seize an opportunity from our familiarity and boldness and produce in us every kind of desire. Sin is capable, even through the touch of a brother's hands or a kiss that is affectionate at first, of secretly rousing the mind of the flesh toward its own ends,

[?] and of opening the eyes of desire wider toward evil, as Adam's eyes were opened after he tasted what pleased him. So even a sister born of the same womb should not continually take her fill of her brother's touches and kisses. Otherwise, I say, a passion that has grown up over time (72) from this constant contact may spring up, especially when the beauty of the body kindles the torches of love ever more brightly in their eyes. Even the secular writer, trying to draw people away from the flame that comes from this, says that the kisses of the beautiful must be guarded against like the bites of venomous creatures. For, he says, the venom of pleasure spreads through the whole body by means of a kiss. That is why it says, 'Greet one another with a holy kiss.' It is as though, in fitting these words together, it were placing the breath (73) of the fleshly kiss within the pure fragrance of the Holy Spirit. 45. I do not think we deserve blame for going even this far in strictness for the sake of the virgin's blamelessness. If sin had not already, in our own lifetime, devised new wrestling-holds within these very relationships, some people might perhaps have blamed us for pressing the argument this far. But sin has been strong enough to devise every form of offence against mothers and daughters through the pleasures of the flesh (just as it held up (74) Amnon to public disgrace for violating his sister). So I do not think those who recommend even this precaution to keep the virgin pure deserve any blame. For the power of attraction (75), I say, that has been implanted in male bodies toward female ones disregards all judgment and draws them together spontaneously, so to speak, even while their thoughts resist within. When female bodies touch female bodies, or male bodies touch male bodies, their natural relation to one another stays unmoved. The exception is someone whose memory is stirred by imagining the person toward whom he naturally felt erotic desire, and who in that frenzy for what is natural to him transgresses toward a relation foreign to it (76). But when a female body touches a male body, or a male body touches a female one, they are secretly excited toward union by one another, even if the souls within them push them away (77) by reasoning. When tow touches tow, or bright fire touches pure fire, there is no smoke. But tow that so much as catches the scent of fire quickly ignites. No great labour is needed, nor anyone blowing from outside, for fire to blaze up from the tow; it has only to come into contact, and at once it has [Notes:] [?] … ἀλογήσασα, κρείσσων καὶ [?]

…the flames [?] kindled. In the same way, a female body touching a male body needs no great effort, nor love blowing it on toward intercourse. Because they have a natural relation to one another, the moment it touches, it immediately has the spark of pleasure smouldering in secret. That is why it says: 'Can anyone bind fire in his bosom and not burn his clothes? Or can anyone walk on burning coals and not scorch his feet? So no one who touches a woman will go unpunished.' The Lord gave himself up for the bride in order to sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water, and to present her to himself in glory, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, so that she might be holy and blameless in both body and spirit. For this reason the virgin, too, ought to be anxious about how to please the Lord, so that she may be holy in both body and spirit. 46. She must not guard against some things while treating others with indifference. Rather, she must hold back from afar, once and for all, every occasion that stains her or produces wrinkles in her. Then she will be holy in body, carrying no defilement from it into the soul, and holy in spirit, muddying it with no thought. For passions do not only pass from the body to the soul. They also begin in the soul, and even when the body is sometimes unable to serve them, I say, they are acted out [?] in the mind through the imagination as though they were being carried out through the body. Think of people who mix water with oil, forcing the qualities of each by their contrivance. They spoil the luminous quality of the oil by stirring it up with the [?] water, and they cloud the clarity of the water by mingling it with the oil. In the same way, those who stir soul and body together through the passions wickedly destroy what is useful in each (78) for life. They muddy the soul, which is luminous and bright, entirely with the slime of the carnal passions that arise from pleasure, and they foul the purity and clarity of the body with this [?], rendering it useless for life. Yet when those liquids are stirred together they lose their natural qualities, but when the disturbance has passed and they have become still, they separate from one another. Each runs back to its own nature as it settles: the oil rests pure on top of the water, and the water becomes its clear vehicle. So too, when soul and body are stirred together by the passions they produce in each other, each corrupts its own nature, being muddied by the other. But once they enjoy stillness, they separate and each withdraws into its own nature. The soul, like a charioteer, displays its luminous beauty, shining down on the body from above. The body, being heavy, settles beneath her as befits her dignity, and becomes her vehicle for her needs here below. 47. So when the virgin sees something of this kind happening in her own constitution [?], she will neither stir up the luminousness of the soul with the passions of the flesh, nor with those from…

…[?] will she allow her own beauty to be confounded. Instead, she will keep each quietly in its own place, order and function, and wisely keep the peace among the parts (79). Having trained both soul and body to remain (80) still according to nature, she will display in its purity the harmonious form that arises from both. She will keep the luminousness of the soul entirely calm and clear, and by ascetic discipline she will keep the form of the body pure of every filthy motion that comes from pleasure. For when the body seethes with gluttony, drunkenness and the pleasures of intercourse, it sends these up against the beauty of the soul. And when the soul is shaken by folly (81) with jealousy and anger, hypocrisy and enmity, it brings these against the body. Sometimes, out of fear of the passions of the flesh, we deaden our bodies to their own passions by fasting and harsh discipline, yet carry around the soul's own passions in a dead body. Then the lameness of our perfection is plain to see, because (82) achieving the one without the other shows the work to be incomplete as far as true virtue is concerned. If we cut away the passions of the body by fasting but leave the soul muddied by its own impulses of jealousy, hypocrisy and the other passions, we do not show the body's discipline to be of any use for virtue. Nor, if we cleanse the soul [?] of its own passions but let the body run loose in the pleasures of the flesh (83) and other luxuries, can we show our life to be perfect in virtue, even if licentious fornication is absent. Whoever means to show a course of virtue pure of all defilement must add the goods of the body to the beauty of the soul, and show the soul's achievements in harmony with the body's ascetic labours. For a life could never prove sincere and true if the members of soul and body lacked harmony and concord with one another. Indeed, I think it is impossible for the goods of the soul to be achieved while those of the body stand in their way, or for the goods of the body to be present unless the goods of the soul lead the way. The soul must be in harmony with itself and bring the body into harmony with itself. Then, with both soul and body moving obediently toward a single course, it will display the blessed life in its perfection. So the virgin will always have her soul resting pure on top of the body, like oil on water, and will guide the body beneath it by the soul's light, like a charioteer. She will mix nothing turbid from pleasure into the beauty of the soul (84), as if from the slime of the body's passions, because she has checked by fasting and ascetic discipline the seething that rises from the body and has purified most of its earthiness through the achievements of self-control. In this way (79) Τοῖς μέρεσι: Reg. 2879 reads τοῖς μέλεσι.

[?] she will pass on to the body nothing disturbed (85) by folly from the passions of the soul that arise from jealousy and hypocrisy. Her life will show a mind clear and luminous, free of all wrath, anger and every improper desire. If she ought to keep the human instrument made of soul and body unmixed with passions, with each part resting in its own nature and performing its own function, then it is fitting that, just as she repels the muddy streams that flow into the body through the belly, she should also turn away those that flow into the soul. In this way each part would remain clear in its natural condition. For as long as the passions trouble the soul, the beauty of virginity cannot be seen undefiled in any way. Rather, she gains nothing from bodily discipline, and much shame from the vice of the passions is seen in her soul. 48. Suppose she has used discipline to settle, like sediment, the slime that rises from the body into the soul, the compulsion of nature, but is then stirred up by the passions within the soul. Then the purity of her body has profited her nothing, since the Bridegroom cannot rest in such a soul because of the turmoil of its passions. Such a woman (86) has rather done herself great harm. Through lack of instruction she has failed to search out what truly pleases the Bridegroom, and through wicked reasoning she has robbed herself even of the reward (87) for her bodily achievements. For if we practise bodily incorruption for the sake of the soul's beauty, the apparent incorruption of the body is pointless while the soul is being corrupted by countless passions. In some people the devil (88) takes the body as an instrument of sin and attacks the soul through it. In others, he has not been allowed to mount the flesh because of their self-control and harsh discipline (89), so he often seizes the naked soul apart from the body and accomplishes his desire through the passions he works in it. Such are the women who drive him out of the flesh by fasting, sleeping on the ground and every other kind of excessive bodily discipline, but cherish him in the soul with the passions of wrath, anger, hypocrisy or jealousy. And as the body is lesser in dignity than the soul, so much lesser, I think, does sin through the body appear than sin through the naked soul. For in the one case, natural nourishment and appetite tickle the body toward gluttony or fornication through the pleasures that accompany them. But in the other, without any bodily pleasure, a wicked will [?] the passions… [Note:] [?] … μισθόν: so four manuscripts; the editions read τῶν [?] … [?].

…For just as love wastes away the soul and body of a lover who fails to obtain his desire, so envy wastes away both the soul and the body of the envious. Lovers who fail to obtain their desire are not wasted by love any more than the envious, failing in their own desire, are wasted in soul and body by envy. They suffer exactly what wax statues would suffer if wax-modellers fashioned them at night and the sun's rays melted them when the sun rose. For as long as night and darkness hold them, they keep their form as it was modelled, set firm in the shade by the night air, with the tautness that shows in the figures, and for the time being they look solid. But when the sun shines out and runs its own course, everything else is nourished by the sun's power and enjoys its light (90), while the statues melt; their forms and shapes, together with the tautness that showed in each, are dissolved, and they vanish. So too the envious. As long as they plot the works of envy in the devil's darkness, as if at night, they seem for the time being to show one another firm intentions and figures with forms, just as envy modelled them. But when a man of zeal rises early like the sun to do the works of virtue, all the others who admire his way of life, which loves what is good and loves God, are brilliantly filled through him with divine love that leads to knowledge, and they nourish the seeds of virtue. The envious, however, see that he is unconquerable like the sun, because he is dear to God, and that he shines (91) still more brightly with the works of virtue, and like wax…

49. The virgin's soul, then, must be calm and unruffled, like a pool filled with divine thoughts from the most pure spring of the mind. It must not be stirred into waves by words that strike it from outside through the hearing, nor have its calm (92) state ruffled by images that strike it through the sight. Then, seeing both her own form and the beauty of the Bridegroom as in a most pure mirror, she may be filled more truly with love for him. So no other face must peer into the mirror of this water, or it will shake the face already there (93) and blot it out. Nor must the water be ruffled in any way by anger or grief or any other passions (94), or in its tossing it will show different shapes to the mind (95) at different times. Rather, the soul must always stay the same, poured out in the joy that comes from God, keeping itself entirely unruffled by passions and showing in itself the form of no one but the Bridegroom… [Notes:] [?] … (91) Λαμπρυνόμενον [?]. (92) Γαληναίαν: all [?] read γαληνήν.

[?] — he alone always seeing his own beauty mirrored in her, and the soul alone having his form shining out in the mirror within her, and wishing to be adorned with the beauty of his form. That is why the most wise Word, making her soul secure, says: “If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, do not leave your place.” This is so that, when a thought of domination comes up, imagination may not find a place, as in a mirror, and, though nothing is present, display the images of sin. Rather, he says, let every place in the virgin’s soul be filled with the sight of Christ. Let no place at all in her lie vacant, where a meddlesome thought might come up and find room to mirror its own images. In short, then, let the virgin’s soul be the mirror of no one, of no man whether present or absent [?], but only of her holy bridegroom. Let no other form be seen in it but his alone. Let her lovingly polish the mirror of her soul for no one else, except so that he may shine into it the image of his own beauty and make her blessed. For if any mortal leans over this mirror, the mind must become busy with gazing at his form, and then it can no longer see the bridegroom’s former form anywhere, since that form has been hidden and has slipped away. And as he who is joined to a harlot is one body with her, so he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him, cleansed of the passions of the body and having sealed the soul into the same form

50. In leading the virgin up to true virginity, we do not plant some notion of marriage in her through the image of the bridegroom. Rather, from the union of marriage we wisely point to the union of the rational soul with God the Word. Bodies, through marital union, come to share in the same pleasures, passions and corruption: in pleasure, in the passions, and in the corruption of intercourse, through their agreement in the act. In the same way the rational soul, through its bridal union with God the Word, would enjoy virtue, incorruption and true freedom from passion in the Spirit. So, through her freedom from passion and her incorruption, and through an unfeigned agreement with God the Word that leads to his holiness, she may become pure. Therefore she who through virginity [is betrothed] to Christ

to meditate on his law day and night. She is to rejoice in the groomsmen, by which I mean the Law and the Gospel and whatever is in harmony with them, as they tell of the bridegroom’s beauty. Through the holy offspring of thoughts begotten by the Word, she is to be found ever more rational and wise, until, wholly and completely united with Wisdom, she becomes one with him to whom she is joined. Then she is shown to all as changed: from corruptible to incorruptible, from ignorant to prudent and wise, as a rib of the Word to whom she was joined. In short, she is changed from a human being into an immortal god, like him with whom she is united. For her bridegroom left thrones and dominions and was joined to her in her mortality, so that, having come to be in her by sharing her sufferings, he might change her into his own freedom from suffering. In the same way she ought to be joined in immortality to him who for her sake stripped off the principalities and powers, and out of love for the bride emptied himself from the form of God into the form of a slave. Then she may also go up with him into the heavenly bridal chamber as he ascends to the Father. “For this reason,” it says, “a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” Interpreting this, the one who betrothed the bride to Christ for her good, for incorruption, says: “This mystery is great; but I speak of Christ and the Church.” For Christ did not come down to be joined to the bride and stay on earth. He came to take her and transform her, and to lead her up from earth to heaven. And she who is wedded to Christ has not only John to serve her at the bridal bath, but also angels singing the wedding song as she goes up to the Father’s hearth. So the virgin not only remains uncorrupted in her union with the incorruptible Word, but even becomes uncorrupted after the union. The bridegroom of bodies corrupts the uncorrupted virgin in marriage and makes her a wife. The bridegroom of our souls does not marry the uncorrupted soul like that, by corrupting her through union with himself. Instead, he receives her from the devil, corrupted through fleshly pleasures and wrongly made the devil’s wife through that corruption, and through union with himself he makes her an uncorrupted virgin again instead of a wife. Teaching us this mystical bridal procession through the prophet as well, he says to his bride: “Did you not call me house and father and author of your virginity?” It is as if he said, “author of your incorruption.” For the husband is the author and ruler of his wife’s corruption, and by this he becomes her lord. In the same way the Lord is the author and ruler of the incorruption of each of us, and through incorruption he is our Lord and takes up his rule. We must also recognize him as the house of our incorruption, remaining and dwelling in him, since

in him we live and move and have our being. So, dwelling in him all our life as a house of every virtue and of incorruption, we may not fall from our hearth of incorruption in him. For as he dwells and walks among the worthy, so in turn the worthy dwell in him. That is why, when he receives us after we have left the affairs of the world, entered into him and settled in him, he takes care that we do not fall away and says: “Abide in me, and I in you.” 51. So too, for everyone else, virginity, when it is understood, is a great and exceedingly splendid thing. It is shown, already here and now, to be a pure seed of the regeneration and of incorruptible life. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels and will become sons of God. If so, those who practise virginity are angels who go about human life in incorruptible flesh. And they are not obscure angels but the most illustrious of all. For the angels, without flesh, keep incorruption in heaven, in their place and in their unextended nature, beside God the King of all. These, on earth, are troubled by the pleasures of the flesh and exposed to the devil’s temptation, and yet through virtue they have kept for their Maker an incorruption equal to the angels’, which is all the more wonderful. Here especially one might marvel at the beauty of virgins. Though clothed in a female body, they have through ascetic discipline driven off the shape that this body impresses on the soul. Through virtue they have appeared equal to men, just as they were in fact created equal to them in soul. Men passed through ascetic discipline from being men into the rank of angels. So these women too pass through discipline from being women into the same dignity as those men. In the present life they are equal to men in soul, though the female covering keeps them from full equality. In the age to come they will be found equal in every respect to those who through virtue have become angels. For if those shown to be equal to angels neither marry nor are given in marriage, then the women who achieve this through discipline in the present life have already shown themselves to all as equal to angels. Through virtue they cut away the properties of female and male, I mean those that serve the union of bodies, and with naked souls on earth [?] (2) “Are given in marriage”: [?] codex reads “ἐγγαμίζονται.”

52. Let such a woman, then, touch the servant of the bridegroom, provided that female pleasure no longer lives in her flesh. Let her welcome her brother without pretence, according to the Lord’s command, washing his feet and caring for another who needs attention, touching a dead body with the dead hands of her body. She has put to death her members that are on earth. She no longer lives; Christ lives in her, and the life she now lives in the flesh she lives by faith. So let her do the works of virtue, with Christ alone living in her and doing his own works, while she carries about a body that is dead and crucified with Christ to sin. And let her do what the bridegroom commands, making the beauty of her soul shine more brightly in every act. For when the body is touched and the soul does not respond to the image of the male, but touches it, so to speak, without feeling, pleasure stays dead in it, since what touches from outside cannot rouse it to its own passion. So too in the persecutions virgins were handed over to impious men because of their faith in the bridegroom. Some were kept uncorrupted even in body. He for whose sake they accepted being handed over proved the attempt of those impious men dead against their flesh, and by miraculous power kept even their bodies, I mean, wholly uncorrupted. Others were assaulted, but their souls had no share in the pleasure, and it was as if their bodies were outraged while dead. Their souls stayed uncorrupted, not shaped to the pleasure of the one who outraged them, and they showed themselves more brightly to the bridegroom in faith and virginity. Perhaps the Lord wished to show in them that they valued confessing him above everything that seems honourable in regard to the body. They did not corrupt their souls by denying him, nor were they wholly corrupted in body, since through the body they had no share in the pleasure. Unless someone would say that a man who, in extraordinary madness, wishes to outrage a virgin who has been slaughtered, corrupts her through intercourse with the dead! He might abuse her, but he could never corrupt her. He corrupts himself and is corrupted, but the virgin is uncorrupted, since her soul is not present. Like her are the women who are harassed by men in persecutions and in every kind of circumstance. Since they have put the flesh to death, whatever they may suffer, they remain uncorrupted. For the time of discipline that came before has trained them well enough for the trial, so that while they live in the flesh they do not wage war according to the flesh. That is why, urging the others to the same virtue, they say: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh.” So let all such women show, I say, also through (6) “Dead”: the Mazarin codex [?]. (9) “Suffer”: [?]. [?] “or like.”

greeting, their love for the brethren. For Mary too, when she kissed the Lord’s feet, did not kiss them as a man’s feet but as the Lord’s. With her tears she wisely quenched and withered the old pleasure of the fire within her, and with her devotion to the Lord and her holy kisses she wisely kindled the spirit in her soul. So she lived by the Spirit and walked by the Spirit, doing everything for the bridegroom with understanding, on behalf of her own sins. But she was dead to sin, having in fear put to death the thought of female and male as she touched his feet and kissed them. 53. Let such a woman touch, then, I say, if there is such a woman anywhere, and fulfil the commandment toward the Lord. But even such a woman, whenever she touches, must wisely keep sober. Otherwise, as she keeps touching, pleasure may creep secretly from the flesh into her little by little. Then, bitten by its venom, she might come to say (God forbid!): “When pleasure came, sin came back to life, and I died; and the commandment of love, which was meant for life, turned out for me to be for death.” For if even angels fall, those equal to angels ought all the more to fear a fall. They have become equal to angels by the discipline of virginity. They must fear that, seeing the daughters of men that they are beautiful, they may come down to them through the pleasures of the flesh, and it may be said to them: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. But you have slipped back into the things of the flesh; you die like men and fall like one of the rulers.” So it is far better for the virgin to keep entirely apart from all mixing with others, securing her own safety and giving no offence to those who see her. She should choose to bear criticism for being awkward rather than [?] for the pleasure and harm of some. She should overlook everything else and look wholly to the Lord alone. And already here and now, from the present life into the age of regeneration, she should display the undefiled beauty of incorruption, equal to the angels and beyond female and male. For virginity gathers us from corruption into incorruption

54. For the first human beings, as I said, from a few seeds sowed the whole earth with humankind through their marriages with one another. But virginity gathers what has been sown across the whole earth through the pleasure of marriage into the storehouses of heaven. Hinting at this gathering of what was sown into incorruption, the Lord said: “Lift up your eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvest.” For the whole world, once uninhabited, had now become inhabited. Our Lord saw the great crop of human beings in every region, already heavy with offspring, and judged that it was now time to gather in these ears of grain. So virginity recognized by nature that, just as the seeds of humankind were cast for the sowing of the present life through the pleasure of marriage,

so too the seeds of our life for the life there are already being cast here through incorruption. It is therefore eager to prepare by itself pure seeds of incorruption for the farmer, for the incorruptible life. With the stronger hand of incorruption it reins back, in the opposite direction, the natural entwining of female bodies with male ones. With a power free of passion it prepares its own beauty to shine more brightly in the age of regeneration. So virgins, by an achievement of virtue, have anticipated what is to be accomplished for them in the regeneration, by the power of God, through the transformation of bodies at the resurrection. Already here, like the angels, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are equal to the angels both in virtue of soul and in incorruption of body. Our Lord willed virginity to be a seed of incorruptible life, sent wondrously from earth to heaven. He wanted our bodies to practise the beauty of incorruption already, through the incorruption of virgins. This is clear from the fact that, though he obeyed the law in everything, marriage alone he renounced. For it was fitting that he who was born uncorrupted, even according to the flesh, from an uncorrupted virgin should not experience the corruption of marriage either. He was not serving corruption of the body through marriage, coming from one who was uncorrupted [?], but serving our natural incorruption, coming from those corrupted by marriage. And as Adam became the seed of the present life through the pleasure of marriage, so he [became] the seed of the age to come through [?] of virginity … [?] … to him who sowed. Just as we followed [Adam], who sowed the earthly life of human beings, so let us wisely follow the Lord, who through virginal incorruption sowed the age there. If you consider Adam carefully, both in paradise and in the life there, you will find that in paradise he had no need to know his wife. But after the transgression, after death and the expulsion from paradise, he then knew his wife, so that he might console his nature, now mortal, with the succession of children. The virgin has followed, in the opposite direction, him who leads into paradise, and already she delights with him, uncorrupted, in paradise. She has escaped the curse outside paradise that says: “In sorrow you shall bear children,” and the rest. And there she cannot grasp [?] how Adam knew his wife. For it was not while he was in paradise, but after he had been cast out, that this

55. We do not say these things in order to lay down virginity as a law for life. But to those who [?] (11) [?] “be cast.” (12) “Not from an uncorrupted [one], by corruption”: so the Venetian edition; [?] read “of human beings.”

have resolved to trade in the precious pearl, we point out how spotless it is in every respect. “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord,” he says, “but I give my opinion as one who has received mercy from the Lord.” For not even our Master, the Lord of nature, laid down virginity as law, either in the Law or in the Gospel. He devised the relation of the male to the female, and in turn of the female to the male, such as the Word showed in the beginning, because marriage was necessary. For those who had become mortal instead of immortal, he provided the succession of the race, and in this, as has been said somewhere, he found a kind of immortality. For this reason he said, “Increase and multiply.” How, then, could he have laid down virginity as law at that time? This is especially true since he saw that a great number of new births was needed to replace those consumed in wars because of their own wickedness. In the law given through Moses, having children was even counted worthy of blessing. But then the world blossomed everywhere with its own fruits. The earth was sown with so great a multitude of people that it could no longer hold the crowd of those being born. And what was prophesied about the coming of our Lord was fulfilled: those wisely persuaded by his teaching will beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles, and nation will no longer take up sword against nation, and they will no longer learn war. Then it was fitting that virginity, in contrast to those corrupted through the body, should make incorruption sprout from bodies. And yet, as I said, the Lord has regard for the nature of male and female bodies, and so he neither lays down virginity as law through Moses nor commands it in the Gospel. Instead, he takes up the law of Moses and teaches what was lacking for exact virtue, saying: “It was said, You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you, Do not even desire,” and so on. He sits on the mountain and opens his mouth with the beatitudes. He goes through the precepts of Moses and raises them all to true virtue, teaches the commandments that lead to salvation, completes his teaching, and comes down from the mountain. Nowhere among the commandments, in either the Old or the New Testament, has he laid down virginity as law. For he wished the achievement of virginity to be not a command but the surplus of a soul that loves virtue. Such a soul, by its own free authority, achieves of itself what goes beyond the commandment and beyond nature. Marriage exists for the sake of nature, and the law prescribes what suits nature. But virginity transcends nature and is not enslaved to law. Beyond the law, it offers the achievement of incorruption to the Maker and Lawgiver. For this reason, I will say again, the Lord nowhere laid down virginity as law. (14) “To trade”: some codices read “ἐμπορεύσασθαι” [?]. (15) “Finding”: one of the Royal codices reads “εὑρόμενος.”

He left it free instead. Man, using his freedom without measure, was forced against nature from incorruption into corruption. So now, by a choice stronger than nature, he might force his own nature from corruption into incorruption. And he does not, I say, lay down this achievement as law or command it. He knows it is something exceptional, beyond nature and beyond law, belonging to a soul that loves virtue. When he heard someone say to him, “It is better not to marry,” he showed how far virginity surpasses nature and said: “Not everyone can accept this.” 56. So too the most divine Apostle, following in his footsteps, lays down in his Epistles what is necessary for life. He adorns the Church in each of its ranks as one body, from the head to the very tips of the nails, as one might say. But about virgins he declares nothing on his own authority. When asked, he imitates the Lord and says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord.” For I find nowhere, either in the Law or in the Gospel, that the Lord commanded this greatest possession of the virtue-loving soul. When the Lord was asked, he answered his questioners, “Not everyone can accept this.” Yet he did not hide either its greatness or the way in which one might achieve virginity, but pointed to it by adding the third kind of eunuch. “So I too, though I have no command of the Lord, still give my opinion.” For where this achievement is to come about beyond nature, every servile command is cast out. Instead, free counsel is brought in at the right moment. It suggests how one who is free of every command, and has become stronger by his own free choice, should wondrously force nature toward incorruption. So as the Lord, when asked, [spoke of] the ways of becoming a eunuch through virginity, so his disciple introduced counsel about virginity, saying: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think, then, that this is good because of the present distress: it is good for a person to remain as he is. Are you bound to a wife?” Were you caught by this bond before you knew the good of virginity? “Do not seek to be released. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.” That is: Do not seek to be tied with a bond. “But if you marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have trouble in the flesh,” since through marriage they open for themselves a workshop of pains. “But I would spare you. This is what I mean, brothers: the time is short from now on.” For the fields are white and already ready for harvest. “So that those who have wives may be as though they had none.” It does not say that those who have none should be as though they had them. Yet some who have no wife, through their promise of virginity, outrage virginity as though they had one. “And those who weep, as though they did not weep;”

...and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing; and those who buy as though not possessing; and those who use this world as though not using it to the full. For the form of this world is passing away. I want you to be free from anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how to please his wife; and he is divided. And the married woman and the virgin are also distinguished. The unmarried woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about the things of the world, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to cast a noose over you, but to promote what is seemly and undistracted devotion to the Lord. But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, if she is past her prime, and it must be so, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin; let them marry. Let him know, however, that she has chosen a mortal husband and the world, for the enjoyment of pleasure, rather than what pleases the Lord. But whoever stands firm in his heart, being under no necessity but having authority over his own will, and has decided this in his heart, to keep his own virgin, will do well. So then he who gives his own virgin in marriage will do well, for it is better to marry than to burn; and he who does not give her in marriage will do better, betrothing her to the Lord instead of to a mortal man. 57. But to those who had learned of the unpleasantness that comes from marriage, who complained that the bond with a wife is hard to dissolve and said, “It is not expedient to marry,” the Lord says: “Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb” — those who, by an advantage of nature, have been cut off from what incites to intercourse, and so despise marriage. “And there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men” — those persuaded by teaching and by being guarded to remain virgins, like the virgin kept by her father, of whom it is said: “But he who has decided in his heart to keep his own virgin will do well.” “And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” These are better than the others, because, having neither a provision from nature toward chastity nor being held in check by men, they train themselves for virginity on their own for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, despising marriage and worldly life for its sake, and holding fast to the whole of the kingdom with an athlete's sweat. For the eunuch from his mother's womb, being chaste by nature, has no work of his own to [Note: Matt. 3:12.]

show in the beauty of virginity, since he turned away from marriage, as I said, by an advantage of nature, and not by a disposition toward virginity. Likewise he who was made a eunuch by men, being compelled by guarding to practise virginity, displays the incorruption of virginity as the achievement not of himself but of those who guard him. But he who made himself a eunuch, making the beauty of virginity his own special work through self-control and discipline in all things, is honoured in the kingdom for his own achievements and not for another's. Note also that in taking up the word addressed to the eunuchs in Isaiah, he hands down the distinction between kinds of eunuchs, keeping to his manner of teaching. For just as through Moses he gave simply the command not to commit adultery, but through the Gospel unfolded how not to commit adultery and the manner of it, so too through Isaiah he spoke of being a eunuch, but in the Gospel showed how, and that being a eunuch is not of one kind only, but that a third kind of it is to be understood; so that there the eunuch is described for us in general, but here in particular. And what has been said does not conflict with what was set out above. For in Isaiah he does not legislate or enjoin being a eunuch, but proclaims what rewards good eunuchs deserve. 58. It is good to examine the words themselves: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that I will, and hold fast to my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my wall a renowned place, better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name, and it will not fail.” So the good things mentioned are not promised to those who are eunuchs by circumstance and merely so, but to those who keep, he says, my Sabbaths, and choose the things that I will. Now the Sabbath is understood to consist not in working but in refraining from action [?]. For he wants the virgin to keep Sabbath, guarding her virginity not by doing something but by keeping her incorruption through remaining unmoved toward activity. The virgin, he says, was fashioned on earth out of soul and body like a statue of God. Let her keep Sabbath in a mystical sense, moving neither hand nor foot nor eye nor any other member, nor even a mind that would destroy her natural beauty; but let her stand like a fine carving of God, unmoved by any fantasy or touch, standing wholly upon the rock; lest someone slip in secretly through the eyes or the hearing or some other single sense, and either disturb the features engraved in the soul after the image of God, or, confusing the originals, wickedly engrave his own somewhere; and so mar the beauty of the soul, and fill the body, which is material, everywhere with stains and blemishes through corrupting touches. Let it stand firm, then, I say, [?] [Note: ἐπισημαίνου (“note”): so five manuscripts; the editions read ἐπισημαίνουσι.]

the Lord's statue, keeping Sabbath completely, so that it neither shifts out of place by moving of itself, nor, in moving, knocks against things and chips off some of its natural features, nor, shaken by a hand from outside, is robbed of the beauty of its nature. 59. Perhaps by the keeping of Sabbath he also hints at how one may possess virginity both naturally and wondrously. For just as, when setting out the definition of our salvation, he says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down), or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” You have no need to busy yourself with things so far from you, with heaven or abysses; rather, you too should use the help that is near and at hand. “For if you confess with your mouth Jesus Christ, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” So too concerning virginity he says: Do not say, “How shall I ascend into heaven to bring down from there the incorruption of my virginity? Or how shall I descend into the abyss to recover for myself what was long ago corrupted by the devil?” But what does it say? It is near you, he says, and virginity is born with you by nature. So you have no need to cross seas to acquire it, nor to fly through the boundless air, nor to track it across the circuits of the earth and measure them out, nor to [?] from earth to heaven to go in search of it; but, as I said, stop busying yourself with distances, examine yourself as you are, and you will find it hidden within you by nature. And if you wish it to remain inviolate with you, keep Sabbath all your life; that is, remain as you were born. Do not move your hand to touch a man, nor plait what is unplaited, nor bind what is loosed, nor corrupt your uncorrupted limbs by entwining them with the limbs of the other sex; but remain on your bed what you are, and busy yourself with nothing more. Keep Sabbath by yourself, doing nothing that would undo what is according to nature. You do not have to leap over walls and enclosures to hunt for virginity. Indeed, by doing such things you might well lose your virginity. But by keeping Sabbath on your bed you will keep it pure, and that easily, [?] [Notes: (30) “Jesus Christ”: three codices read “the Lord Jesus.” “Of virginity”: two codices read “of incorruption.”]

how will that which has received knowledge of a man be reckoned as not having received it? How will what has once been wounded by desire and pleasure and passion become again as though unwounded, when the marks of corruption remain wholly in the soul and in the body? For repentance remits sin; but being unable to make the corrupted woman uncorrupted again, she mourns all her life. Therefore, since this possession is very great, and the prize for those who achieve it most glorious, let us, persuaded by the Lord's teaching, keep Sabbath as the word has suggested from beginning to end, keeping the natural beauty of the divine statue wholly undefiled and untouched by any stain. Let the virgin, he says, not only keep Sabbath, but also choose the things that I will. And what else does the Lord will but incorruption?
