When, after keeping Sabbath, she has chosen this, by comparing the corruption in marriage with the incorruption in virginity, and holds fast to the covenant with the Lord in the commandments, she will receive from him, in his house and within his wall, a renowned place, the one better than sons and daughters. For not only to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths and choose what I will, but also to those who hold fast to my covenant, will I give what has been said. So the virgin ought to remember the covenant of the Bridegroom night and day, the covenant which he made in writing for her incorruption when he died for her. And remembering the covenant in his death for her, that he gave himself up for her in order to sanctify her, let her hold fast to his covenant throughout her life; that is, let her not set aside the dispensation accomplished in his death for her salvation. For since she had sold off her own freedom, he bought her back with his own blood; and having bought her back, he not only honoured her with freedom, but, betrothing her to himself as a bride, deigned by surpassing grace to make her a queen. Therefore let her hold fast to his covenant; that is, to put it more plainly, since the marriage was established in writing and lawfully, by his covenant with her as by a kind of dowry contract, let her always hold to the stipulations and terms of their life together, presenting herself blameless to him in all things, so that, having lived worthily with him here, she may also enjoy the good things he gives there. 60. For to those who keep my Sabbaths (I will say it again), he says, and to those who choose the things I will, and who hold fast to my covenant, I will give in my house and within my wall a renowned place, better than sons and daughters. For lest they seem to be disgraced as seedless and childless, they shall be, he says, my own household and friends, so that they remain in my house and within my wall. And they will be judged by me worthy of such great honour that no nobility of offspring could vie with the place of their dignities. For I will give them [Notes: [?] “her own”; the Paris manuscript [?] “within the wall”; some codices [?]]

a place, he says, not only of dwelling but also of advancement and rank, so that, being conspicuous to all, it will dignify them with the nobility of rank beyond any succession of children. And what more, he says, can I say about the mystical eunuchs? I will give them an everlasting name, which will suffice them in place of a succession of descendants, and it will not fail. For here the children of bodies, taking on their fathers' name, succeed to their life as it is quenched by old age, and so too, entering into it, they rekindle in themselves the failing name of fathers who are being carried off to death. Then, having for a short while consoled in this way the life and the name of their ancestors' line, they are nevertheless dissolved by their mortal nature, and they too, as time goes on, will fail entirely, leaving the line without a name. But the name I give to the eunuchs, together with a place among the foremost, will suffice completely, I say again, in place of any succession of the line, so that they themselves and all who see them will declare from the outcome how surpassing it is, that it is truly better than sons and daughters, who often bring blame upon the family, with a place of shame and a name of sin. For I will give them, he says, instead of a human name, the name of the immortal angels, and it will not fail; so that they have heaven, and the fairest part of heaven, as their dwelling. And dwelling in the fairest part of heaven, that is, in my house, within its enclosures, they will henceforth have not only the nature and immortal rank of angels, so as to have no need of succession (since they always suffice in themselves, in an ever-living life, in place of successors for ever), but also the most distinguished place among the angels, and a name that cannot be erased, because of the splendour of their achievement. But let them take care that, as they ascended from men and earth to heaven and the rank of angels, they do not likewise fall the greatest of falls from the angels and heaven down to earth. For I saw, he says, him who once flashed in the heavens fall like lightning from heaven. Hearing this, they ought to take care in every way. Such, then, are the rewards that the eunuchs who are divine in mind will be found worthy of in the kingdom. Nor will those miss the like who were forcibly made eunuchs in childhood by a tyrant's hand. But if, in the involuntary bodily castration that befell them, they make themselves eunuchs by a voluntary castration of the mind, so as to keep Sabbath against all vice, to choose what the Lord wills, and to hold fast to the covenant of his commandments, then, being found not barren of virtue in soul, they will have a place in the house of the Lord better than sons and daughters; no longer regarded as a dry tree because of their childlessness in the flesh, but as flourishing plants [?]

adorned on every side with many fruits of righteousness. For planted, he says, in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God. So, I say again, he did not legislate virginity, but leaving it to free choice, he showed, by way of mystical castration, what those who have outstripped nature deserve. 61. But those who did not understand the words, “And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,” have absurdly mutilated themselves, by the very deed proclaiming their own licentiousness from afar. For those who threw away the weapon of carnal desire so that it might not act if it were present plainly show that they are driven toward intercourse, but, having disarmed themselves, remain virgins not because they do not wish to but because they cannot. Yet the divine law judges not the act but the intention; for everyone — not the one who committed adultery in deed, but the one who looked in order to desire — has already committed adultery. And cutting off the parts convicts the man who is cut of adultery more than does desire in the eye. For, distrusting himself as to whether he will master his licentiousness, he cut off that by which he would carry out the act of desire. Or rather, being convinced that if it remained he would act without restraint, he disarmed the instrument of licentiousness by cutting it off, so as not to seem licentious in the body; yet he is licentious nonetheless in desire, and without restraint commits adultery with every woman. For the attempt itself cries out from afar against his incontinence. That is why one might say that such men become more licentious after the cutting. For, unable to master themselves, and then afraid of being caught in the act, so that they may be free to indulge desire as they wish, being slaves of pleasure, and not wanting the result of the act to become a hindrance to their continual enjoyment, they cut off the proof of the deed and give themselves unrestrained license for intercourse. Now if a man who brings a sword against someone wearing a breastplate is nonetheless punished as a murderer, even though the breastplate prevents the blow and the killing; and if a man who wished to bring a sword against someone unarmed, but then through some circumstance dropped the sword from his hand, is justly judged a murderer, because the law judges not the deed but the will; then the man who is armed with the generative member, even if he made the attempt and could not corrupt as he wished the woman armoured with faith, deserves punishment as though he had corrupted her; just as the man who found a woman unprotected against corruption and rushed at the deed, but cast away the weapon by cutting it off, so that the corruption did not take place, is justly judged as one who accomplished the corruption. In this case she too is found to be accused with him of licentiousness, and not without reason. For how shall we believe that she would have repelled the blow of corruption brought by the licentious man if the weapon had been present? Where she struggles [?] stoutly for her incorruption against a man naturally armed, the contest of chastity is evident. But where the man is unarmed and she is indifferent toward him,

or rather where their association flows toward pleasure out of attachment, her chastity is unclear to all, and licentiousness carries off most of everyone's votes against her. But this concerns those who have cut off the parts entirely together with the testicles. For those who, after reaching manhood and being ready for intercourse, cut off only the testicles of the generative parts are said to be goaded more fiercely and uncontrollably toward intercourse; and not only goaded, but, as it seems to them, able to corrupt without risk the women they come upon. For they say that when the testicles below are cut off — which serve as conduits of the seed from the loins and kidneys to the remaining member — the passages above close after the cutting; but as desire boils in the kidneys and froths up the seed there, the man is goaded to discharge the seed, and having no way to drain off the seething semen, he is armed for the act by that which he preserved for himself for intercourse. And having cunningly made the removal of the testicles a bait to deceive the woman, he couples with her more licentiously. For the man in his natural state, when the testicles have received the seed from above and sent it on from there for sowing, is spent once the seed has been discharged, and his desire withers away; but the man who has nowhere to empty out the tickling scarcely lets up from his labour, until exhaustion, they say, releases him from his frenzy. To this not only the reasoning of nature but also experience in our own life has testified, as a certain venerable man, old both in grey hairs and in manner of life, declared to me after a woman had confessed to him. For he said that the woman had told him that the eunuch to whom she had been entrusted by her husband, or her master, had intercourse with her licentiously like a man. And he was all the bolder in the act, she said, trusting in his sterility, since no child would result. Not only he, but also another man of like mind with us, who would not readily lie, said that a canonical virgin of the Church lamented to him that a certain eunuch, having got into her bed, embraced her passionately, and clinging to her with his whole body, since he had no means of performing the acts of desire, used his teeth, savagely showing by his bites the frenzy for intercourse boiling in his flesh; and that the virgin, having been entangled in the temptation through her innocence by the bait of his being a eunuch, after the experience turned away from the man, and lamented not only to this man but to many others the defilements of that man's desire against her. And the testimony of two men is true, so that we need not list many others and go on longer than we would like. [Notes: (45) Οἰστρεῖσθαι (“to be goaded”): so the manuscripts; the editions read οἰστροῦσθαι. (46) [?] ἐξαφανιζούσης.]

62. We deserve pardon, then, I think, for setting these things out not only to safeguard the virgin's purity, but also in an effort to check the many eunuchs of this kind who have already sprung up in the Church. For it is plain that this is the work of a demon's cunning. Long ago he paraded such men in the way of life of the Greeks, and now, absurdly, among us; there he gave castration the name of self-control, and here too he has brought in the same innovation against nature. For the one who schemes against our faith in the Lord is clever at working evil through the very good that people trust, and one can learn this from the past as well. Among the Greeks he arranged that the very things through which they ought to have known God should make them ignorant of him. (For the world stands before them as a sign of the one who adorned it. Yet they did not reason from the beauty of the things they saw to the beauty of their Maker and glorify him, but worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.) In the same way he contrives that the very things through which people ought to know Christ should make them ignorant of him. I mean the Scriptures that proclaim Christ: through heretical notions he cleverly engineers ignorance of Christ out of them. And just as he craftily sows unbelief in Christ and denial of him by means of the trusted name of Christ, so also, by means of the name of mystical eunuchhood, he produces men who are both castrated and licentious, and calls it self-control. So it is not fitting for the virgin to mingle freely with these men either. Women who embrace women intimately in the same bed, with the heat of youth seething within them, are often stirred by the contact of their bodies to remember the bodies they were formed to have relations with. (For the one who makes sin a law in our members is able to slip secretly into the midst of the flesh, steal away the friendly and affectionate pleasure that women take in one another, and cunningly sow in its place the male pleasure of the flesh.) If that is so, how much more must the virgin guard against male bodies, even those of eunuchs? For though he is a eunuch, he is still a man by nature. 63. A butting ox whose horns have been cut off has not become a horse by losing its horns. It is still an ox, even without horns. So too a male who has cut off all his parts has not become a woman by losing them. He is still male by nature, even without the parts. And a butting ox with its horns cut off is still a butter in temper. It bends its neck, shapes its head for the charge, and eagerly shows its threat; but [Editor's note: ὑπέδειξε: other editions read ἀπέδειξε; the printed editions, ἐπέδειξε. (56) ἄρσην: [?] in this place and a little further on.]

it has often struck with the part of the head that was armed with the horn, satisfying its temper with the imagined act. That is how it is affected when its impulse carries it away: it does not feel it is striking a mere blow, but goring with the horn as before. So too the male whose parts have been cut off is male in his desire for the passion. That is why he too, shaping himself in the same way for the act, breathes out love and outlandish madness. Moreover, when he rushes toward intercourse, he may not corrupt the woman by troubling her with that part. Yet in his desire, under the power of his imagination, he feels as if he had corrupted her. And by provoking her more bitterly toward sin, he corrupts her whole mind and goads her body as well toward the act of corruption. 64. Therefore, if the virgin's aim is to keep the virginity within her uncorrupted, let her always be strict about her dealings with these men too. For we also accept the counsel of Sirach as contributing to the virgin's purity: "Like a eunuch," he says, "embracing a virgin and groaning." He groans, of course, because he cannot do what he wants. And again: "The lust of a eunuch to deflower a young woman." For even if he does not make her a mother, because he is sterile, still, he says, he wants to deflower her. It is not right, then, to praise those who cut off their parts for their self-control. We do not praise horses for not butting; we will praise them if they do not kick. But oxen, if they do not butt, we will rightly commend for their gentleness. For a person is admired not for what he cannot do, but because, though able, he has not used his power for wrongdoing. But if they think that cutting off the parts contributes anything to the soul's sinlessness, let them also gouge out their eyes, which look at many things they should not. Let them cut off their hands and their feet as well, and stop up their hearing, so that none of these may become an instrument of sin. Or rather, this is senseless and mad. It means lopping off every member on every side and, as the saying goes, throwing away the rest of the body like a useless stump, along with what caused the sin, while still letting the mind sin through the images it has already received through the members. Instead, as man was formed, according to the argument above, we should guide all our members with the reins of sober reason, so that our good achievement comes not from compulsion but from our own choice. We have not said all this about every eunuch, but about those who have absurdly castrated themselves to gain the freedom to associate with women as they please. And in general we say these things about all who seek out the company of women. For we know that just as men touch women in holiness, [?] looking [?],

so too there are eunuchs who associate purely with women. To the involuntary eunuchhood that befell their bodies they have added a voluntary eunuchhood of the soul, making themselves eunuchs by sober reason. But for the sake of strictness and purity we declare this: men who are too fond of spending time with women rightly bring shameful suspicions on themselves, and in the same way eunuchs who are eager to nestle into the company of women do not clear themselves of suspicion. For those who are not indifferent to the company of women but over-eager for it might reasonably be denounced as worse than men, on the natural grounds set out above. In the case of men, the power to act puts the outcome of the sin before their eyes, and the fear of falling holds them back from the sin they intend. But in the case of eunuchs, their inability to accomplish what they want makes them bold in enjoying their desire, and so it kindles the sin of intention in them all the more. 65. Let no one mock this discourse for delving into the nature of the male in a way unbecoming to a virgin's character. First, no virgin who has come to maturity of body is so childlike as to be ignorant of anything in the nature of him from whose side she was taken. As long as the members of her body are immature and not yet ready for their natural activity, the law of sin is idle, and perhaps one might say that for the time being her members are ignorant of the natural act. Even so, nature makes its own way toward what belongs to it, as can be seen in the irrational animals: taught by nature alone, they at once find their way to mating. Children too have been caught imitating male intercourse while their members were still immature. But once these members have matured and are seen to be fit for the relation they were made for, the law of sin immediately enters. It lays down the act as a law for each member, sets the members at war against the law of the mind, and through the members takes each person captive to the law of sin. With the law as its teacher, no member could plead ignorance of the sin it was formed for. The lips know their use in love-making, and each member knows the corresponding member of the other sex as well as it naturally knows itself. Otherwise it would not have desired that member's activity, if it had not known its nature and use. So we do not deserve blame for unfolding at the proper time what virgins know but leave unspoken out of necessity. Second, even if they are ignorant of the male's emission, we have examined nature as it is so that this very ignorance may not become a bait

drawing them to sin. It was not unreasonable to do so for their safety: just as they are innocent as doves, so also, being wise as the serpent, they may be prompted by the teaching set before them to guard in advance against every wrong done against their incorruption. Besides this, since we are making our discourse a means of purifying virginity in general, we owe it in goodwill to men as well as to virgins. Just as we showed the virgins what harms and what helps, it was necessary to show the men as well. Then they will not fix their attention on the mere name of eunuchhood and fall into the opposite. Instead, recognizing the sin that comes from unlawfully cutting off the parts, and knowing what kind of eunuch the Lord counts worthy of acceptance, they will be helped toward true eunuchhood of the mind. And those who over time have absurdly multiplied through the irrational impulse to cut off their parts will be checked by this discourse and sensibly held back. 66. If, then, the true virgin lives with such strictness, she will keep herself wholly pure of all male touch. Even when she sleeps among women, she will turn inward and keep her mind in heaven. Having placed her mind entirely outside the body, she will say the same as the one who said: "I know myself—whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows—that I was caught up into paradise and heard unutterable words." For the Bridegroom sees from heaven above her wakeful love for him. He sees that she makes the darkness of night not a provision for sin but leisure for divine converse with him. She is clothed in the darkness of night so that her senses are not troubled by things outside; she is illumined by the Bridegroom's light; and all night long, in secret, she lovingly adorns her whole mind and his lamp. So he will rightly catch her up too as far as the third heaven, into paradise, and will speak to her such things as have been declared unutterable to those still living in bodies. But to her, who has advanced so far that she no longer knows whether she lives in the body or outside it, they will become utterable in a mystery. Wishing and praying that the whole choir of virgins may be found like this, I have gone through what has been said as a safeguard against those who defile the beauty of virginity. My purpose was not that by studying these things we should learn how to slip toward what harms [Editor's note: (66) ὡσεί ("as"): [?] reads ὡς αἱ. A little earlier some codices read οὕτω καὶ τοῖς [?] παισὶν [?].]

[?] but that, having learned [the] power [of these things], they may guard against them with opposing powers, and if these do somehow befall the body, may destroy them by knowledge. There are three ways, then, which our Lord pointed out as leading us to virginity, according to the third kind of eunuchhood; and he says, "Let whoever is able to accept it accept it," by whichever way he wishes. She who travels toward virginity by one of the other two ways is acceptable too; but she who runs by the better way is more blessed. Yet let all who press on toward it, by whatever way, take equal care to be blameless on the road. Then, having betrothed the bride to the Bridegroom pure of every stain, they will enjoy his gifts all the more gloriously in heaven. 67. These things, holy head, I have written to you as time allowed, so that you may understand the beauty that truly belongs to virginity. I drew them not only from the divine writings but also from outside sources. For, following the most wise Paul, I wish us to take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ, and I want every disciple of Christ to be shamed into self-control. The wise men of the Greeks, too, hinted at the many forms of pleasure and the battle against it by means of a myth. They invented the Hydra, a many-shaped creeping thing lurking in a marsh, which they explained allegorically as the general pleasure that resides in the body. They handed down the story that when one of its heads was simply cut off, three grew in place of the one; but they showed, philosophically, that a head cut off with a cautery was destroyed once and for all. Pleasure in general always lurks in the material nature of the flesh, like some terrible reptile in a marsh. Through each sense it rears up, as if a single head rose from the depths, taking many forms in the pleasure of sight, of taste, and of the rest. If, they say, we try to cut off each head by enjoying its particular delight to the full, we will not so much cut off the head that appeared as make more grow in place of the one by this way of cutting. But if we cut out the head that appears with self-control, as with a cautery, we will wisely destroy it once and for all, so that it never sprouts again. Suppose someone wishes, they say, to destroy the pleasure of taste by satiety, by giving it the delight it wants. He has not so much destroyed it as made it, through enjoyment, ever more unrestrained toward what it desires. But he who punishes it with self-control as with fire, by refusing it the delight, has rendered it once and for all inactive and wasted away, since it does not get what it longs for. And superfluous, they say, or rather harmful to ascetic practice, is the saying that flatly declares that what is readily available stirs no desire. For the pleasure of taste is idle, [Editor's notes: (72) ταύτην: the Paris edition alone reads πρὸς ταύτην. (74) πολυμόρφως ἡδονήν: so [?] codices, much more fittingly than the printed editions, which read πολυμόρφων ἡδονήν. (77) τετηγμένην: the printed editions read τετμημένην [?].]

let us say, toward what it has the power to enjoy. But having always been taught to use without restraint its power to enjoy whatever it wants, it is drawn on insatiably and in many forms to exercise that power over everything it desires. Therefore, they say, one should not cut off each head of pleasure in that way, but by endurance, refusing to gratify the delight. 68. The divine Word, too, when it sacrificed the calf for the priesthood in the writings of the most wise Moses, showed allegorically, through the parts that were burned whole, the way of ascetic practice. It commanded that the lobe of the liver be burned whole, and not the whole liver; the fat covering the belly, and not the belly itself; but in the case of the kidneys, not only the fat but the kidneys themselves along with the fat. For the liver is the organ of desire. (That is why it is said of one wrongly struck with desire, "You will be like a stag struck in the liver by an arrow.") So we should burn whole, like the lobe, only the particular desire that leads to sin, in which the bile is also found, and keep the rest, pure of bile and of wicked desire, for the natural desire for good things. In the case of the belly, we should remove the excess by which we grow fat toward irrationality and keep only what is necessary. But in the case of the kidneys, we should consecrate not only the fat—the great abundance of seed that foams up into licentiousness—but the kidneys themselves. In this, I say, he spoke in a most natural allegory about what is necessary for life, what in desire loves the good, and what is pure for self-control. For since it is impossible to live in the body without food, he leaves the organ of nourishment, the belly, bare and free of all gluttony, and fittingly removes the fat that covers it. Again, since we cannot possess any good thing without having a natural power of desire toward it, he cuts away the base kind of desire, like the lobe with the bile, and leaves pure the good kind, the desire for the virtues. As for the kidneys, since they are seen to be necessary neither for life, as the belly is, nor for desire in general, but receive only the particular desire for sexual intercourse, he hands over to the fire not only their fat but the kidneys themselves,

[teaching us] to offer our bodies as a holy sacrifice, well-pleasing to God, like the calf for the priesthood, and to consume with the divine fire of self-control, in one case wicked desire, like the lobe; in another the excess of food, like the fat covering the belly; and in another the whole desire for marital intercourse altogether, like the kidneys together with the fat that supplies them with seed. Then, in keeping with the aim of virginity set before us, we will be shown through ascetic practice to be stronger than every base desire and every pleasure, and will be found worthy of the prize set before us in the contest and of the crown of incorruption, through Jesus Christ, through whom be glory to the Father also, with the Holy Spirit, for ever.
